result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of improving generalization in deep reinforcement learning across diverse environment variations, observing that policies trained broadly (generalists) learn quickly early but plateau suboptimally while narrowly trained policies (specialists) can reach higher returns with limited compute. The key insight is that combining the strengths of both—using a generalist for fast broad learning and specialists for focused mastery—can overcome the generalist’s plateau and boost overall performance. The proposed method first trains a generalist on all variations, then, once progress stalls, spawns many specialists initialized from the generalist and each trained on a small subset of variations, and finally continues generalist training augmented with auxiliary rewards derived from specialists’ demonstrations; the paper also studies when to start specialists and how best to incorporate their assistance, demonstrating improved results on Procgen, Meta-World, and ManiSkill.

result.text: The paper challenges recent criticisms of unitary scalarization—simply minimizing the sum of task losses—in multi-task learning by showing that with standard single-task regularization and stabilization techniques it matches or outperforms many specialized multi-task optimizers across common supervised and reinforcement learning benchmarks. The key insight is that much of the perceived need for complex, per-task-gradient optimizers can be mitigated by careful application of regularization and training stabilizers, and that many bespoke multi-task methods can be interpreted as introducing implicit regularization rather than solving fundamentally different optimization problems. Methodologically, the authors compare unitary scalarization augmented with established regularizers and stabilizers against a suite of state-of-the-art multi-task optimization algorithms, analyze the relationship between those algorithms and regularization effects, and empirically demonstrate comparable or superior performance while avoiding the memory, runtime, and implementation overhead of per-task-gradient methods.

The key insight is that only a subset of test samples—those that are reliable and non-redundant—should be used for adaptation because high-entropy samples produce noisy gradients, and that constraining changes to important parameters prevents forgetting. The method actively selects low-entropy, diverse test samples to perform entropy-minimizing updates and applies a Fisher-based regularizer (with Fisher importance estimated from pseudo-labeled test data) to penalize large updates on critical parameters, yielding faster adaptation with lower backward-pass cost and preserved performance on in-distribution data.

result.text: The paper addresses the gap between current LLM research—focused mainly on using given tools—and the agent-like capability to decide whether to use a tool and which one(s) to pick from a set to satisfy user requests. Its key insight is that tool-use in agent settings requires both “tool usage awareness” (knowing when to invoke any tool) and nuanced tool selection across challenging scenarios (similar options, context-specific needs, reliability concerns, and multi-tool coordination), which existing LLMs largely fail at. To quantify this, the authors introduce MetaTool, a benchmark and dataset called ToolE containing single- and multi-tool prompts, define tasks and four subtasks for selection evaluation, and evaluate eight popular LLMs to reveal performance gaps and error modes. Based on results and analysis, they offer practical guidance—notably that tool developers should tailor description rewrites to the downstream LLM—to help improve tool-selection behavior.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of reliably and comprehensively evaluating modular Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, whose long-form outputs and separable retrieval and generation components make measurement difficult. The key insight is that a fine-grained suite of diagnostic metrics that separately assesses retrieval and generation behaviors—and that are validated against human judgments—provides more faithful and actionable evaluation than existing holistic metrics. The authors introduce RAGChecker, a framework that defines and computes multiple targeted metrics for retrieval quality, grounding, faithfulness, and generation quality, and demonstrate via meta-evaluation that these metrics correlate better with human judgments; they then apply RAGChecker to analyze eight RAG systems, revealing trade-offs and design patterns to guide system development.

result.text: The paper tackles causal representation learning when observations are only partially informative—each measurement reveals a subset of latent causal variables and the observable subset can vary per instance—challenging standard identifiability assumptions that all latents are always reflected in data. The key insight is that an instance-dependent sparsity pattern in how latents mix into observations provides a principled constraint that enables identifiability: under either linear mixing with minimal assumptions or piecewise-linear mixing with Gaussian latents, the true causal factors can be recovered. Methodologically, the authors derive two theoretical identifiability results and develop two corresponding estimation algorithms that encourage sparsity in the recovered representations to match the partial-observability structure. Empirical results on synthetic and benchmark datasets show these sparsity-enforcing methods more accurately recover ground-truth latent variables than prior approaches.

result.text: The paper tackles the latency and compute blowup in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) caused by linearly increasing input length as more documents are retrieved. Its key insight is that most retrieved documents are irrelevant to each generation step, so encoding them in parallel and then sparsely selecting a small subset to attend to during autoregressive decoding can preserve quality while cutting computation. The proposed Sparse RAG encodes all retrieved documents independently into caches, prompts the LLM with special control tokens to assess and choose highly relevant caches on the fly, and then decodes by attending only to those selected caches, thereby merging per-document relevance assessment and generation into a single process. Empirical results on short- and long-form tasks show this sparse mechanism reduces the number of documents loaded during decoding, accelerating inference and often improving generation by filtering out distracting context.

The key insight is that instead of concatenating retrieved neighbors to the input, one can fine-tune the model at test time on a small set of nearest-neighbor training examples using the model’s usual training procedure, which yields large gains even with very few gradient steps and neighbors. Concretely, the authors build a large distributed embedding index over the Pile, retrieve ~20 nearest neighbors per test input, and perform one gradient update per neighbor (test-time training) before evaluating, showing substantial improvements across 20+ language modeling tasks and dramatically closing the gap between small and much larger models, provided the retrieval index is sufficiently large and high-quality.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of applying Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to real-world document analysis, where source materials are long, unstructured HTML/PDFs containing text and tables that complicate retrieval and LLM-based question answering. The key insight is that existing RAG pipelines and LLM solutions perform variably across document domains and query types, and that upstream choices—especially data parsing and retrieval strategies—substantially impact answer quality. To study this, the authors introduce UDA, a benchmark of 2,965 real-world documents and 29,590 expert-annotated Q&A pairs spanning academic and financial materials, and systematically evaluate popular LLM- and RAG-based methods to compare design decisions and their effects. Their results reveal practical failure modes and guidance for improving RAG for unstructured documents, and they release the benchmark and code to support further work.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem that empirical risk minimization (ERM) often yields models with high average accuracy but poor performance on certain groups due to spurious correlations, and that methods which ensure high worst-group accuracy typically require costly group labels. Its key insight is that the examples ERM misclassifies early in training are disproportionately from poorly served groups, so upweighting those examples when training a second model can improve worst-group performance without needing group annotations. The proposed method, JTT, first trains a standard ERM model for a few epochs to identify misclassified training examples, then trains a second model that upweights those hard examples; only a small labeled validation set with group annotations is needed to tune hyperparameters. Empirically on four vision and NLP tasks with spurious correlations, JTT recovers the majority of the worst-group accuracy gap between ERM and group DRO while avoiding per-example group labels.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of distribution shift—specifically subpopulation and domain shifts—where models trained on one distribution fail on shifted test distributions. Its key insight is that invariant predictors can be learned not by constraining internal representations but by selectively augmenting data via mixup: interpolations that either combine samples with the same label from different domains or with different labels from the same domain encourage invariance without restricting model internals. The proposed method, LISA, implements this selective mixup strategy during training, producing augmented examples that guide the model toward predictors that generalize across domains and subpopulations; experiments across nine benchmarks show consistent improvements over prior methods and theoretical analysis in a linear setting demonstrates reduced worst-group error.

result.text: AgentBench addresses the lack of a standardized, multi-dimensional evaluation for using large language models (LLMs) as agents in interactive environments by providing a benchmark of eight diverse tasks that probe reasoning and decision-making under multi-step, API-driven interactions. The key insight is that while top commercial LLMs already perform well as agents, many open-source models (≤70B) lag substantially, primarily due to deficiencies in long-term reasoning, decision-making, and instruction-following rather than model size alone. To quantify these gaps, the authors evaluate numerous API-based and open-source LLMs across the curated environments, analyze common failure modes, and show that improving instruction-following and training on high-quality multi-round alignment data can meaningfully boost agent performance, whereas code-oriented training yields mixed effects depending on task type.

result.text: The paper tackles hallucination in large multi-modal models (LMMs), where models produce image-inconsistent or instruction-inconsistent descriptions, by creating the first large, diverse visual instruction tuning dataset designed to train and evaluate robustness. The key insight is that including carefully constructed negative instructions—queries that prompt nonexistent-object claims, manipulations of existent objects, or incorrect knowledge—alongside positive examples forces models to learn to refuse or correct hallucinations and that a balanced mix improves robustness. Methodologically, the authors build LRV-Instruction (400k GPT-4-generated instructions across 16 tasks) containing both positive and three semantically distinct negative types, introduce GAVIE (GPT4-Assisted Visual Instruction Evaluation) to measure hallucination without human ground-truth, and finetune MiniGPT-4 and mPLUG-Owl on this dataset, demonstrating reduced hallucination and improved performance on public benchmarks.

The method introduces FIND, a suite of textual and numeric functions with ground-truth descriptions, and evaluates pretrained LMs both in one-shot description and in an interactive Automated Interpretability Agent (AIA) setup that iteratively hypothesizes, experiments on black-box functions, and refines descriptions; results show the AIA captures global behavior well but often misses fine-grained local details, highlighting FIND’s utility for developing more sophisticated interpretability methods.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem that large language models often produce suboptimal outputs on their first pass and lack a simple, training-free way to improve them at inference time. The key insight is that the same LLM can act as generator, critic, and refiner: by producing an initial output, self-generating feedback on its shortcomings, and using that feedback to iteratively refine the output, quality can be improved without additional data or training. The method, called Self-Refine, runs this loop of generation → self-feedback → refinement repeatedly with a single LLM (e.g., GPT-3.5, ChatGPT, GPT-4) and is evaluated across seven diverse tasks; it yields consistent improvements over one-step generation, with about a 20% absolute average gain by human and automated metrics.

result.text: The paper tackles the fundamental ill-posedness of Causal Representation Learning (CRL), which aims to recover hidden causal variables and their relations from observational data but typically requires strong assumptions like temporal structure, interventions, or supervision to be identifiable. Its key insight is that identifiability can instead be achieved via a weak structural constraint on the observed mixing: observational variables can be partitioned into groups that each depend on only a subset of latent causal factors, and this grouping suffices to pin down the latent causal representation without temporal or interventional information. Methodologically, the authors formalize a generative model with grouped observational variables, derive identifiability results under these grouping conditions, and propose a self-supervised estimation framework tailored to the model; they prove statistical consistency and empirically demonstrate improved CRL performance and robustness to latent confounders and cycles compared to prior methods.

result.text: The paper addresses the foundational question of when deep unsupervised latent-variable generative models—specifically decoders used in practical VAEs with universal approximation capacity—are identifiable from observed data without any auxiliary or side information. The key insight is that under broad architectural and prior conditions common in practice (e.g., mixture priors in latent space, ReLU/leaky-ReLU activations, and universal approximation decoders), the full generative model can be recovered from x alone and different modeling assumptions yield a hierarchy of identifiability guarantees (ranging from identifiability up to affine transformation to stronger, nearly unique recovery). Methodologically, the authors prove a series of theoretical identifiability results that generalize prior conditional or supervised identifiability theorems to the unsupervised setting, characterize how assumptions (activation type, prior structure) determine the strength of identifiability, and validate their theory with experiments on simulated and real datasets.

result.text: The paper tackles the open problem of mechanistically explaining how a real-world language model accomplishes a nontrivial linguistic task—indirect object identification (IOI)—rather than toy behaviors or only high-level descriptions of large models. Its key insight is that GPT-2 small performs IOI via a distributed but tractable “circuit” composed of 26 attention heads that cluster into seven functional classes whose causal roles can be probed and characterized. Methodologically, the authors combine multiple interpretability tools—notably causal interventions, ablations, and quantitative metrics for faithfulness, completeness, and minimality—to identify, group, and validate these heads’ contributions to IOI and to measure how well the proposed circuit explains model behavior. The results show a largely faithful, reasonably complete, and compact explanation while highlighting residual gaps, arguing that mechanistic reverse-engineering of realistic language-model behaviors is feasible and scalable.

result.text: The paper addresses how to learn shared representations for multi-task reinforcement learning that capture both commonalities and task-specific differences while avoiding redundant or collapsed features. Its key insight is that enforcing orthogonality among expert-generated representations encourages diversity and a compact shared subspace that can be flexibly combined to represent different tasks. The proposed method, Mixture Of Orthogonal Experts (MOORE), builds a mixture-of-experts encoder whose expert outputs are orthogonalized via a Gram–Schmidt process to form a shared subspace, and a task-conditioned gating mechanism selects relevant combinations from that subspace to produce task-specific representations for policy learning. Evaluated on MiniGrid and MetaWorld, MOORE outperforms prior baselines and achieves state-of-the-art performance on MetaWorld.

result.text: The paper tackles the vulnerability of test-time adaptation (TTA) methods to noisy, unexpected samples in unlabeled test streams—scenarios like unseen objects or corrupted inputs where existing TTA algorithms can be misled by blindly adapting to every incoming example. The key insight is that robustness requires screening out harmful inputs and stabilizing parameter updates: selectively adapting on high-confidence, class-uniform samples reduces the influence of outliers, while minimizing an entropy-sharpness objective guards parameters against destabilizing large gradients. The proposed method, SoTTA, implements input-wise robustness via high-confidence uniform-class sampling to filter test data and parameter-wise robustness through entropy-sharpness minimization during adaptation, and experiments on standard TTA benchmarks with various noisy conditions show SoTTA outperforms prior methods under noise while matching their accuracy on clean streams.

result.text: The paper tackles object hallucination in large vision-language models (LVLMs), where models describe objects that are not present in images, undermining tasks like visual summarization and reasoning. The key insight is that hallucination arises from predictable statistical factors—object co-occurrence patterns, decoder uncertainty, and a tendency for hallucinated items to appear later in generated text—which can be exploited post-hoc to reduce false mentions. The authors propose LURE (LVLM Hallucination Revisor), a model-agnostic, post-processing algorithm that re-scores and reconstructs generated descriptions by accounting for co-occurrence priors, uncertainty signals, and positional cues to suppress unlikely objects. Evaluated on six open-source LVLMs, LURE yields about a 23% improvement on object-hallucination metrics and ranks highest in both GPT and human evaluations.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of making large language models interpretable across multiple granularities rather than offering only local or global views, with the additional goal of enabling actionable interventions at inference time. Its key insight is that imposing sparsity can reveal meaningful, compact structures across three linked layers—input features, subnetworks (model components), and high-level concepts—so that explanations are both more faithful and more actionable. The proposed method, SparseCBM, enforces sparsity to extract and link salient input tokens, a sparse subnetwork responsible for predictions, and concept activations, and it supports interpretable inference-time interventions that modify sparse components to correct or probe model behavior. Empirical evaluations on real-world datasets show that SparseCBM yields clearer holistic explanations and can improve model outputs by targeted, interpretable adjustments during deployment.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of ballooning Key-Value (KV) cache size and the resulting memory/time costs when LLMs process very long contexts. The key insight is that individual attention heads consistently attend to a small set of prompt positions and that this head-specific attention pattern can be predicted from a short “observation” window at the end of the prompt. SnapKV leverages this by clustering and selecting the important KV positions per head (without finetuning) and only storing those compressed KV entries during generation, yielding similar accuracy while keeping decoding latency stable and dramatically reducing memory use. Empirically, SnapKV speeds decoding ~3.6×, improves memory efficiency ~8.2× on 16K inputs, scales to ~380K tokens on a single A100 with negligible accuracy loss, and maintains baseline performance across 16 long-context datasets.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of reliably identifying functionally important features in neural networks, noting that conventional sparse autoencoders (SAEs) often capture dataset structure rather than directions crucial to the network’s computation. The key insight is to train the sparse dictionary end-to-end so that the learned sparse codes are constrained to preserve the original model’s output distribution—measured by minimizing the KL divergence between outputs of the intact model and the model with SAE-reconstructed activations—thereby forcing the dictionary to capture features that are actually functionally relevant. Methodologically, they augment SAE training with this KL objective and compare e2e SAEs to standard SAEs, showing Pareto improvements: e2e features explain more of network performance, use fewer total features, and require fewer active features per example while retaining interpretability, and they release code for reproducing the experiments.

result.text: The paper tackles hallucinations in large vision-language models (LVLMs), where models generate incorrect or ungrounded text, without relying on costly extra data or doubling inference. Its key insight is that pretrained LVLMs can introspectively judge the importance of visual tokens conditioned on prior vision and text context, so selectively removing unimportant vision tokens early can amplify text-informed hallucination signals that reveal vision-text associations. The method, Self-Introspective Decoding (SID), uses a Context and Text-aware Token Selection (CT2S) strategy to prune unimportant vision tokens after early layers, computes amplified hallucination logits driven by the remaining vision-text association, and subtracts these from the original token logits during autoregressive decoding to suppress aimless visual hallucinations. Experiments show SID reduces hallucinations and improves text quality across metrics without extra knowledge sources and with minimal added computation.

result.text: The paper tackles slow LLM inference caused by mutual waiting in speculative decoding, where a fast draft model generates token candidates and a slower target model must verify them but both stall due to asynchronous execution and fixed draft lengths. The key insight is that overlapping drafting and verification by verifying the first draft token early (pre-verify) and allowing the draft model to continue producing additional tokens during verification (post-verify) lets the two phases run in parallel and enables an adaptive draft length tailored to runtime conditions. The proposed method, PEARL, implements these strategies so the draft model pre-verifies its first token while still drafting and the verifier post-verifies to extend drafts, dynamically adjusting how many tokens are proposed, which reduces idle time and mutual waiting; experiments show up to 4.43× speedup over autoregressive decoding and 1.50× over vanilla speculative decoding.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of polysemanticity in neural network internals—where neurons respond to multiple distinct concepts—by testing the hypothesis that this arises from superposition, i.e., features being distributed across overcomplete directions rather than single neurons. The key insight is that sparse autoencoders can discover an overcomplete basis of activation-space directions that are both sparsely active and more monosemantic (interpretable) than traditional neuron- or PCA-like decompositions. Methodologically, the authors train sparse autoencoders to reconstruct language-model activations, evaluate the learned features with automated interpretability metrics, and demonstrate that these features allow finer-grained causal attribution (e.g., on an indirect object identification task) than prior decompositions. The results suggest a scalable, unsupervised approach to resolving superposition and producing more human-understandable components for mechanistic interpretability.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of keeping large language models up-to-date through efficient online adaptation without costly continual fine-tuning, addressing scalability in time and memory as new documents arrive. result.text: The paper studies how well offline reinforcement learning (RL) agents generalize to new environments compared to online RL, sequence modeling, and behavioral cloning, motivated by the fact that prior work trains and tests on the same environment. The key insight is that many state-of-the-art offline RL and sequence-modeling methods generalize poorly to unseen levels or instructions, and that behavioral cloning—especially when trained on diverse multi-environment data—can outperform more complex offline methods on both train and test environments. To demonstrate this, the authors construct the first benchmark for offline generalization using Procgen and WebShop datasets with varying dataset sizes and skill distributions, evaluate a broad set of algorithms under train/test environment shifts, and show empirically that diversity of data, not mere scale, drives improved generalization.

result.text: The paper tackles the failure of existing test-time adaptation (TTA) methods when unlabeled test data arrive as temporally correlated, non-i.i.d. streams (e.g., in autonomous driving) rather than the commonly assumed i.i.d. setting. The key insight is that adapting batch statistics and sample selection to account for out-of-distribution instances and class imbalance in the incoming stream can restore reliable adaptation under temporal correlation. Concretely, the authors introduce Instance-Aware Batch Normalization (IABN) to correct normalization for OOD or shifted samples and Prediction-balanced Reservoir Sampling (PBRS) to maintain a class-balanced reservoir that simulates an i.i.d. stream from a non-i.i.d. sequence, and they integrate these with TTA training updates. Experiments on several datasets, including real-world non-i.i.d. streams, show the method substantially improves robustness over prior TTA approaches while matching their performance in i.i.d. scenarios.

result.text: The paper addresses hallucinations in large vision-language models (LVLMs), where generated text can diverge from image content, noting that existing visual contrastive decoding methods fail to reliably suppress hallucinatory tokens due to uncontrolled global visual uncertainty. The key insight is that contrastive decoding’s effectiveness depends on precisely amplifying the preference gap between hallucinated and target tokens, which can be achieved by replacing noisy global uncertainty signals with a learned, theoretically grounded preference model to more accurately identify and penalize hallucinatory outputs. The authors propose Hallucination-Induced Optimization (HIO), which fine-tunes a Contrary Bradley-Terry preference model to amplify contrasts between hallucinatory and correct tokens and then uses this model to guide contrastive decoding, thereby more effectively discouraging hallucinations. Experiments across multiple benchmarks show HIO reduces hallucinations and outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods.

result.text: The paper tackles slow speculative decoding for LLM inference, where a smaller draft model currently generates tokens autoregressively and spends equal time on all tokens, causing inefficiencies and limited speedups. The key insight is that removing autoregressive drafting and reallocating drafting effort non-uniformly across tokens can greatly reduce wasted computation while still preserving the target model’s output distribution. The proposed Cascade Speculative Drafting (CS Drafting) introduces a Vertical Cascade that replaces neural autoregressive token-by-token generation with parallel or non-autoregressive drafting, and a Horizontal Cascade that dynamically prioritizes and allocates drafting time to more important or uncertain tokens; combined, these cascades let the target model accept larger portions of drafts less frequently and thus run fewer iterations. Empirically, CS Drafting attains larger inference speedups than prior speculative decoding methods while maintaining the same output distribution as the target model.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of improving language model performance with retrieval without incurring the training-vs.-inference mismatch and the quadratic cost in Transformer computation/memory from appending large retrieved contexts at test time. The key insight is that instead of concatenating retrieved neighbors to the input, one can fine-tune the model at test time on a small set of nearest-neighbor training examples using the model’s usual training procedure, which yields large gains even with very few gradient steps and neighbors. Concretely, the authors build a large distributed embedding index over the Pile, retrieve ~20 nearest neighbors per test input, and perform one gradient update per neighbor (test-time training) before evaluating, showing substantial improvements across 20+ language modeling tasks and dramatically closing the gap between small and much larger models, provided the retrieval index is sufficiently large and high-quality.

args.text: We propose Counterfactual Activation Sharpness (CAS) decoding for LVLMs: a training-free, test-time method that penalizes tokens whose likelihood is fragile to targeted visual perturbations but stable to text paraphrases. CAS builds counterfactual mini-batches by selectively pruning unimportant vision tokens early in the network and by paraphrasing the prefix; for each candidate next token it estimates a Hallucination Fragility Score as the variance of token logits across visual counterfactuals minus that across text counterfactuals, normalized by an internal-activation sharpness/consistency measure. This score is then used to reweight logits during decoding—optionally combined with a lightweight preference model—thereby suppressing visually ungrounded continuations while preserving instruction consistency. By unifying introspective token selection with internal-representation diagnostics and principled contrastive reweighting, CAS targets object and attribute hallucinations with minimal overhead and without extra data.

result.text: The paper addresses why reinforcement learning agents often fail to generalize from limited training environments to unseen test conditions, arguing that the sequential decision-making setting creates a distinct challenge not captured by supervised-learning generalization analysis. args.text: Cross-Modal Alignment Sharpness (CMAS) Decoding: a test-time control for LVLMs that penalizes tokens whose next-step vision–text alignment is "flat." After early layers, we apply SID-style context- and text-aware pruning of uninformative vision tokens to amplify grounding signals; we then compute an alignment-sharpness score by combining (i) an eigen-gap of the covariance of attention-weighted visual features across heads/layers (capturing INSIDE-style semantic concentration) and (ii) hidden-state entropy sharpness over in-context tokens. This score subtracts from token logits during autoregressive decoding or guides contrastive re-ranking, suppressing hallucinated objects/instructions without extra data or doubled inference. By unifying introspective pruning with activation-based sharpness, CMAS targets cases where visual grounding is weak despite fluent language, reducing LVLM hallucinations across settings.

The hypernetwork is trained to distill the effect of gradient-based test-time training on retrieved neighbors, while also learning to route or compose from a library of reusable adapters for further efficiency. At inference, the frozen base LM is modulated by the generated adapters, and a patience-calibrated exit head halts computation on easy inputs, preserving most of the gains of retrieval TTT at a fraction of the latency. This combines the accuracy benefits of retrieval-driven adaptation with amortized modulation and adapter reuse to yield scalable, compute‑aware online adaptation.

Its key insight is that adaptation can be achieved without changing model weights or computing gradients by optimizing an added input prompt and selectively shifting activations using a derivative-free evolution strategy guided by a fitness function combining test-vs-training statistic discrepancy and prediction entropy. args.text: Counterfactual Activation-Gap Decoding (CAGD) for LVLMs: At each decoding step, compute a grounding score by measuring the change in hidden-state sharpness and eigen-spectrum between the normal forward pass and a counterfactual pass with visual tokens masked or pruned; tokens whose predictive distribution barely changes are flagged as text-driven and penalized. Concretely, we adopt SID-style context- and text-aware token pruning to keep salient vision features, then compute layer-wise entropy-sharpness and INSIDE-style EigenScores for candidate tokens across the full vs counterfactual passes, and subtract a learned preference-weighted gap from logits during decoding. A small contrary Bradley–Terry head trained on negative-instruction style data calibrates the penalty, yielding targeted suppression of ungrounded continuations without extra training of the base LVLM. The same counterfactual principle applies to text-only LLMs (e.g., RAG) by contrasting with evidence-masked runs, offering a unified, low-overhead mitigation of hallucination.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of slow inference for long-context large language models, where self-attention becomes bottlenecked by loading a large key-value (KV) cache as sequence length grows. The key insight is that only a small subset of KV cache tokens are critical for a particular query and that token criticality depends on the query vector, so one can predict which cache pages matter without scanning the whole cache. They propose Quest, a query-aware KV cache page selection algorithm that maintains min/max key summaries per cache page and uses the query to estimate page criticality, loading only the top-K pages for attention; this approach yields large self-attention and end-to-end latency speedups (up to 2.23x and 7.03x respectively) with negligible accuracy loss on long-dependency tasks.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of recurrent neural network (RNN) world model backbones in model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL), namely their limited long-term memory when simulating future observations in partially observable environments. Its key insight is that alternative sequence models—Transformers and Structured State Space (S4) models—offer complementary strengths for capturing long-range dependencies, and that S4 in particular can provide superior long-term memory and efficiency for latent imagination. The authors introduce S4WM, the first S4-based world model capable of generating high-dimensional image sequences via latent rollout, and perform extensive comparisons of RNN-, Transformer-, and S4-based world models on specially designed benchmarks testing long-term imagination, context-dependent recall, reward prediction, and memory-based reasoning. Empirically, S4WM outperforms Transformer-based world models on long-horizon memory tasks while requiring less computation during training and imagination, suggesting S4 is a promising backbone for stronger MBRL agents.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of recovering latent variables and their causal structure from observational data when observed variables are generated by causally related, potentially unobserved, nonlinear latent factors arranged in a hierarchical graph. Its key insight is that under mild structural assumptions—allowing multiple causal paths between variables and permitting general nonlinear, multi-dimensional continuous structural functions—latent variables and the causal graph are identifiable up to invertible transformations, even when some latents have no observed children. Methodologically, the authors first derive an elementary identifiability criterion for a basic latent variable model, then leverage this criterion to construct an explicit estimation procedure that asymptotically recovers both the latent variables and the hierarchical causal structure, providing the first identifiability guarantees for this class of nonlinear latent hierarchical models.

args.text: Epistemic-gated generalist–specialist MoE for RL: train a soft-MoE generalist whose router conditions on a compact belief over latent environment parameters estimated by an ensemble (epistemic POMDP), so routing and data partitioning follow uncertainty structure rather than surface variation. Continually distill the generalist’s behavior into a lightweight actor for deployment on constrained hardware, preserving the transformer learner’s sample efficiency while meeting latency. Evaluate on procedurally diverse benchmarks expecting improved zero-shot generalization from uncertainty-aware routing plus specialist-assisted learning.

We propose a forward-only, safe test-time adaptation scheme for temporally correlated streams that couples derivative-free prompt/activation search with reliability-aware sample scheduling. A prediction-balanced reservoir approximates an i.i.d. buffer from the stream, and adaptation is triggered only on samples whose augmentations yield low marginal-entropy and high consistency, further enforcing class-uniformity and OOD-aware filtering. We then run brief CMA-ES steps to tune a small prompt/shift vector and validate each step on the reservoir, rolling back when an entropy-sharpness surrogate (e.g., increased average marginal-entropy or augmentation-variance) degrades, avoiding collapse without backprop or fragile normalization. This unifies forward-only adaptation with safe selection and buffering, using augmentation consistency as a cheap reliability signal for robust, resource-constrained, non-i.i.d. TTA.

ShadowTool is an emulator-guided, cost- and risk-aware toolchain selector for LLM agents: it prunes and ranks candidate multi-step tool plans before any expensive real invocations. It combines tree-of-plans generation with an LM-based tool emulator and safety evaluator to cheaply simulate alternatives, while a contextual reliability prior fit on real tool traces and fine-grained progress signals estimates per-step success and value-of-information. At decision time it maximizes a utility over completion likelihood, failure risk, and latency/monetary cost, with toolkit-level routing for redundancy and automated contrastive prompts when uncertainty is high. Evaluated on tool-selection benchmarks and end-to-end real-tool tasks, ShadowTool aims to cut real tool calls and catastrophic failures without sacrificing accuracy.

result.text: The paper addresses when and how unsupervised object-centric representations can be learned provably from visual scenes, filling a theoretical gap behind empirically successful methods. Its key insight is that if the scene generation satisfies two properties—compositionality (the scene is generated by composing object-specific factors) and irreducibility (object factors cannot be further decomposed)—then the true object representations are identifiable even when objects are dependent. The authors prove that an inference model that is both invertible and compositional recovers the ground-truth object factors under this generative model, validate the theory on synthetic datasets, and show that existing object-centric methods’ empirical identifiability correlates with their measured compositionality and invertibility.

result.text: The paper tackles the KV-cache memory bottleneck in LLM decoding, where storing key-value pairs for all previous tokens limits deployment and existing pruning/eviction schemes hurt tasks needing long-range recall. The key insight is that adding a tiny, constant-sized recurrent cache that synthesizes and preserves summarized recurrence can complement eviction-based caches so that no token is truly unrecoverable, allowing the model to query approximate historical information without storing all KV pairs. The method, called LESS, integrates a nearly-free fixed-size recurrent cache with standard eviction or pruning strategies: during decoding LESS maintains and updates a compact summary representation of past states while evicted full KV entries remain removable, enabling the decoder to reconstruct or approximate older context when needed. Experiments show LESS substantially narrows (and sometimes closes) the performance gap with full caching across diverse tasks while drastically reducing memory use.

result.text: The paper addresses Continual Test-Time Adaptation (CTTA), where a source model must adapt to continuously changing unlabeled target domains without access to source data, a setting in which self-training with noisy pseudo-labels leads to error accumulation and catastrophic forgetting. The key insight is to shift adaptation from altering model parameters to learning lightweight image-layer visual prompts that reformulate inputs for the frozen source model, thereby preserving source knowledge while capturing domain-specific shifts. The method designs two complementary prompt types—domain-specific prompts to encode current-domain characteristics and domain-agnostic prompts to retain shared knowledge—and introduces a homeostasis-based adaptation strategy that suppresses domain-sensitive parameters in the agnostic prompts to better learn invariant features. This model-free prompt learning approach avoids forgetting and error accumulation and yields substantial gains over prior CTTA methods on CIFAR-10C, CIFAR-100C, ImageNet-C, and VLCS benchmarks.

args.text: We propose a risk-aware, toolkit-level planner for LLM tool agents that maintains per-tool reliability and latency models learned from an LM-based tool emulator and on-policy execution logs, then uses these models to steer planning away from tail-risky toolchains. At inference, the agent first samples diverse high-level plans and then grounds decisions on an abstracted toolkit graph, optimizing a tail-risk objective over task failure and budget overrun while enabling rapid intra-toolkit substitutions when errors occur. Before executing each high-risk step, it auto-rewrites candidate tool descriptions with a contrastive comparator tailored to the current model and query to disambiguate near-duplicate tools and reduce selection mistakes. Evaluated with stepwise progress metrics on realistic multimodal, real-tool tasks, the approach aims to cut catastrophic failures and token/time waste versus strong baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses the persistent problem of object hallucinations in large vision-language models (LVLMs), where models generate visually inconsistent or non-existent object references. The key insight is that hallucinations can be reduced by jointly leveraging fine-grained local grounding to correct tokens as they are produced and a global search strategy to favor grounded hypotheses during sequence decoding. HALC implements this by adding an auto-focal grounding mechanism that dynamically assesses and rectifies token-level visual alignment, combined with a specialized beam-search decoding that re-ranks beams based on grounding consistency, and it operates as a plug-and-play decoding module requiring no additional training. Experimental results across four benchmarks show that this dual local–global approach lowers object hallucinations while maintaining generation quality, outperforming prior methods.

args.text: Query-Aware Retrieval and Cache Scheduling (QuARCS) is a RAG decoding scheme that jointly routes attention over retrieved-document caches and the model’s own KV cache pages at each token. Building on Sparse RAG’s per-document cache gating, QuARCS adds a query-conditioned pager like Quest to load only the top-K KV pages and uses ZipCache-style normalized attention proxies computed by a tiny draft step (run in PEARL-style overlap) to prefetch the next-step document caches most likely to be needed. A tiny recurrent summary cache (LESS) shadows both the conversation and each retrieved document, enabling aggressive eviction of rarely used caches while preserving recoverable long-range recall. This tight coupling of routing, prefetch, and speculative overlap reduces IO stalls and context distraction, targeting end-to-end speedups with equal-or-better grounding quality versus Speculative RAG.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of "narrow vision" in mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, where the gating mechanism routes inputs so strictly that individual experts see limited data and underfit their sub-tasks, constraining overall generalization. args.text: We propose a conservative contextual bandit controller for test-time adaptation that selects, per-batch, among a toolkit of lightweight primitives (e.g., TTN-style moment interpolation, sharpness-aware entropy minimization, and forward-only prompt/activation shifts) using context features like uncertainty, augmentation consistency, OOD scores, and class-imbalance indicators. The controller optimizes an unsupervised surrogate reward that blends entropy reduction with stability/sharpness penalties and agreement on a small class-balanced replay reservoir to counter non-i.i.d. streams, while enforcing a safety constraint that rejects actions predicted to harm an in-distribution memory buffer, yielding online regret-style guarantees. This compute-aware policy learns when to adapt, how aggressively, and with which primitive under mixed, noisy shifts, outperforming fixed-method baselines and avoiding collapse. The approach is plug-and-play, wrapping existing TTA modules and learning the scheduling policy online without labels.

args.text: We propose Detector-Guided Decoding (DeGuD) for LVLMs that reduces object hallucination by coupling autoregressive text generation with on-the-fly open-vocabulary detection. At each step, candidate noun/attribute tokens are grouped into phrase hypotheses and verified by a frozen open-vocabulary detector (e.g., OWL-ViT/GLIP), producing region-grounding scores that are fused with LVLM logits via a posterior-regularization term and a coverage-consistency prior; unsupported mentions are downweighted or deferred. Unlike internal-attention grounding or contrastive decoding, this external verifier provides calibrated, localized evidence and can be used training-free or with a small preference head to learn fusion weights from hallucination/grounded pairs. DeGuD complements HALC’s local–global grounding and LURE’s uncertainty/position cues and is expected to excel on crowded scenes and long captions where co-occurrence priors dominate.

result.text: The paper tackles causal representation learning when observations are only partially informative—each measurement reveals a subset of latent causal variables and the observable subset can vary per instance—challenging standard identifiability assumptions that all latents are always reflected in data. The key insight is that an instance-dependent sparsity pattern in how latents mix into observations provides a principled constraint that enables identifiability: under either linear mixing with minimal assumptions or piecewise-linear mixing with Gaussian latents, the true causal factors can be recovered. Methodologically, the authors derive two theoretical identifiability results and develop two corresponding estimation algorithms that encourage sparsity in the recovered representations to match the partial-observability structure. Empirical results on synthetic and benchmark datasets show these sparsity-enforcing methods more accurately recover ground-truth latent variables than prior approaches.

args.text: We propose Speculative KV-Gated RAG, which unifies speculative decoding with query-aware document-cache paging to minimize retrieval IO and context bloat. A lightweight drafter jointly proposes next-token spans and, at each step, gates only the most critical pages from pre-encoded per-document caches, using query-conditioned page scoring and normalized-attention saliency; the verifier accepts spans and pages in an overlapped pipeline, expanding the gate only on low-confidence cases. This merges sparse, per-step document selection with draft-and-verify so the large model rarely loads irrelevant caches, reducing latency and improving robustness to distractors. The design integrates sparse RAG selection, speculative RAG-style verification, and query-aware KV/page saliency to tightly couple retrieval budgeting with token acceptance.

Train causally aligned k-sparse transcoders: replace each transformer MLP with a sparsely activating transcoder and add an interchange-intervention objective that aligns individual latent units to variables in a task-level causal model. result.text: The paper tackles the practical limitation of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) for serving foundation models to diverse, real-time workloads where each request may require a different task- or user-specific adapter, which conventionally prevents efficient batching and thus hurts throughput. The key insight is that LoRA’s low-rank parameterization can be restructured so that distinct adapter weights can be applied per example within a minibatch without duplicating full-model copies, enabling simultaneous processing of heterogeneous adaptations. They implement this idea as Fast LoRA (FLoRA), a framework that tags each input with its corresponding low-rank matrices and executes batched, adapter-specific forward passes using optimized tensor operations, and they show it preserves LoRA’s effectiveness on MultiPL-E code generation across 8 languages and multilingual speech recognition across 6 languages.

args.text: We propose compiling natural-language task descriptions into executable reward programs that operate directly on a world model’s latent states, yielding dense, cheap signals for imagination-driven RL. result.text: The paper examines Test-Time Adaptation (TTA), addressing the problem that inconsistent experimental settings and limited evaluations obscure the true robustness and limits of TTA methods under distribution shift. The key insight is that prior promising results hide three pervasive pitfalls—hyperparameter and model-selection sensitivity tied to online batch composition, strong dependence of TTA efficacy on the pre-trained model’s quality and properties, and the lack of any single method that reliably handles all common shift types even under ideal conditions. To demonstrate this, the authors introduce TTAB, a comprehensive benchmark that evaluates ten state-of-the-art TTA algorithms across diverse distribution shifts and two protocols, and they run extensive experiments that reveal these failure modes and call for broader, more rigorous evaluations and a re-examination of underlying assumptions in TTA research.

args.text: We propose Counterfactual-Grounded Contrastive Decoding (CGCD) for LVLMs, which unifies token-level causal visual grounding with internal-activation trust signals to suppress object hallucinations at test time. At each decoding step, CGCD estimates a causal grounding score for candidate object/attribute tokens by grouping visual tokens into regions and measuring logit deltas under region-masking counterfactuals, then fuses this with sharpness/consistency statistics from hidden states to quantify hallucination risk. The risk adaptively subtracts penalties from candidate logits and guides a global beam re-ranking pass, while a lightweight co-occurrence prior only penalizes late, low-grounding mentions to avoid hurting fluency. This plug-and-play procedure amortizes cost via grouped perturbations and early token pruning, and is expected to outperform SID/HALC/LURE by only suppressing prior-driven tokens when internal evidence indicates ungroundedness.

args.text: Interchange-constrained Sparse Feature Circuits (IC-SFC): train sparse dictionaries or transcoders not only to preserve the original model’s outputs but also to satisfy causal abstraction tests via interchange interventions, so that each latent/subcircuit is tied to a verified causal variable in a task-level model. During training, we impose interchange-equivalence constraints on individual latents and use gradient-based edge pruning to identify the minimal edge set mediating each latent’s effect, yielding compact, faithful per-feature circuits with reduced polysemanticity and edit-ready structure. We will evaluate on GPT-2-small’s IOI and the greater-than mechanism, and use an automated interpretability agent to propose counterfactual prompts and targeted variable swaps for systematic testing. We hypothesize IC-SFC improves intervention minimality, compositionality, and transfer across prompts compared to standard SAEs or unconstrained circuit discovery.

We propose a Latent Reward Compiler that converts natural-language task specs into temporal reward checkers operating directly in a world model’s latent space, enabling cheap, dense feedback during imagination and planning. Concretely, we align language and vision to the generative world model’s latents (à la GenRL) and use an S4-backed world model for long-horizon rollouts; we then supervise a compact latent temporal verifier by distilling signals from VLM-based rewards and VLM-synthesized reward code evaluated on pixel reconstructions of imagined trajectories, augmented with counterfactual rollouts to break spurious correlations and reduce modality-gap artifacts. The resulting verifier runs at every latent step without VLM calls, supports tree search or online RL, and yields robust prompt-following across 2D/3D embodied tasks with improved sample efficiency and generalization.

result.text: ShadowTool is an emulator-guided, cost- and risk-aware toolchain selector for LLM agents: it prunes and ranks candidate multi-step tool plans before any expensive real invocations. It combines tree-of-plans generation with an LM-based tool emulator and safety evaluator to cheaply simulate alternatives, while a contextual reliability prior fit on real tool traces and fine-grained progress signals estimates per-step success and value-of-information. At decision time it maximizes a utility over completion likelihood, failure risk, and latency/monetary cost, with toolkit-level routing for redundancy and automated contrastive prompts when uncertainty is high. Evaluated on tool-selection benchmarks and end-to-end real-tool tasks, ShadowTool aims to cut real tool calls and catastrophic failures without sacrificing accuracy.

args.text: We propose object-centric causal representation learning under multi-view partial observability with environment-wise sparse interventions viewed as compressed-sensing codes over slots. Building on identifiability from shared multi-view structure, instance-dependent sparsity in mixing/observability, and compositional object factors, we show that if the view-by-environment intervention/masking design satisfies a simple cover/RIP-like condition, then object-level causal variables and their interventional effects are identifiable up to slot permutation. We instantiate this with a slot-contrastive multi-view encoder that uses environment-indexed FiLM and group-lasso regularization to match interventional signatures across views, leveraging environment-driven parameter changes in polynomial SEMs to estimate mechanisms. Compared to prior object-centric sparse-perturbation methods, this removes the need for labeled targets or full visibility and predicts identifiability per slot via a combinatorial algebra over the view-environment design.

result.text: Query-Aware Retrieval and Cache Scheduling (QuARCS) is a RAG decoding scheme that jointly routes attention over retrieved-document caches and the model’s own KV cache pages at each token. Building on Sparse RAG’s per-document cache gating, QuARCS adds a query-conditioned pager like Quest to load only the top-K KV pages and uses ZipCache-style normalized attention proxies computed by a tiny draft step (run in PEARL-style overlap) to prefetch the next-step document caches most likely to be needed. A tiny recurrent summary cache (LESS) shadows both the conversation and each retrieved document, enabling aggressive eviction of rarely used caches while preserving recoverable long-range recall. This tight coupling of routing, prefetch, and speculative overlap reduces IO stalls and context distraction, targeting end-to-end speedups with equal-or-better grounding quality versus Speculative RAG.

result.text: Uncertainty-routed specialist distillation for scalable RL generalization: start by training a broad generalist, then use ensemble-based epistemic inference to cluster environment variations into latent regimes and spawn specialists initialized from the generalist for each regime. result.text: We propose a risk-aware, toolkit-level planner for LLM tool agents that maintains per-tool reliability and latency models learned from an LM-based tool emulator and on-policy execution logs, then uses these models to steer planning away from tail-risky toolchains. At inference, the agent first samples diverse high-level plans and then grounds decisions on an abstracted toolkit graph, optimizing a tail-risk objective over task failure and budget overrun while enabling rapid intra-toolkit substitutions when errors occur. Before executing each high-risk step, it auto-rewrites candidate tool descriptions with a contrastive comparator tailored to the current model and query to disambiguate near-duplicate tools and reduce selection mistakes. Evaluated with stepwise progress metrics on realistic multimodal, real-tool tasks, the approach aims to cut catastrophic failures and token/time waste versus strong baselines.

result.text: The paper tackles hallucination in large multimodal models—erroneous text output that is inconsistent with visual input—by proposing a decoding-time fix rather than retraining. The key insight is to use the model’s own detailed, self-generated descriptions of the image as contrastive references: comparing candidate continuations against those descriptions helps identify and suppress tokens that deviate from the actual visual content. The method, COuntering DEscription Contrastive Decoding (CODE), computes token-level adjustments during decoding by dynamically reweighting next-token probabilities based on similarity to the self-generated description versus the primary prompt-conditioned distribution, thereby steering generation toward outputs aligned with the visual counterpart. CODE is a plug-in contrastive decoding strategy that requires no extra training and empirically reduces hallucinations and improves cross-modal consistency across multiple benchmarks.

args.text: We propose identifiable object-centric multi-view causal representation learning under occlusion and unlabeled sparse interventions. Each view observes a nonlinear mixture of a subset of objects, and episodes provide pre/post pairs where a single object property is perturbed but the object identity and affected view(s) are unknown. By combining object-level compositional irreducibility with the multi-view identifiability algebra, we show the object latents and cross-view correspondences are uniquely recoverable (up to permutation) when each object is visible in at least two views across episodes and receives occasional perturbations; we instantiate this with contrastively aligned slot encoders whose slots predict which views registered the change. result.text: We propose compiling natural-language task descriptions into executable reward programs that operate directly on a world model’s latent states, yielding dense, cheap signals for imagination-driven RL. Combined with long-memory S4-style world models and GenRL-style latent grounding, the resulting "latent reward code" can supervise long-horizon planning entirely in imagination and be reused across tasks as affordance libraries. Its key insight is that a sufficiently capable LM can emulate tool execution and interpret agent-tool interactions, allowing large-scale, low-cost simulation of diverse tools and scenarios without needing to instantiate each real tool. The method, called ToolEmu, pairs an LM-based tool emulator with an LM-driven safety evaluator to generate test cases, emulate tool responses, run agents against those emulations, and automatically classify and quantify resultant failures; human evaluation shows 68.8% of emulator-flagged failures correspond to real-world failures, and analysis of a 36-tool, 144-case benchmark reveals substantial risk even among the safest agents (23.9% failure rate).

args.text: We propose an identifiability algebra for object-centric multi-view causal representation learning under occlusion: when each view reveals only a subset of objects, the co-visibility hypergraph across views and scenes can guarantee recovery of object-wise causal latents up to per-slot reparameterizations. Concretely, under a compositional-and-irreducible object generative process and smooth view-dependent mixing, identifiability holds if (i) the co-visibility hypergraph is pairwise-connected (every slot chain-co-occurs across some sequence of view subsets) and (ii) each slot experiences at least one sparse, slot-targeted perturbation across the dataset—or, alternatively, instance-dependent sparsity of slot visibility provides sufficient support variation. We instantiate this with a contrastive, multi-view slot encoder that enforces cycle-consistent slot matching on the co-visibility graph and a causal-loss that anchors which slot changed under interventions, yielding stronger guarantees and fewer required perturbations than monolithic encoders. This unifies multi-view partial-observability, object-centric structure, and sparsity/interventions into a single theoretical and algorithmic framework.

result.text: We propose Speculative KV-Gated RAG, which unifies speculative decoding with query-aware document-cache paging to minimize retrieval IO and context bloat. A lightweight drafter jointly proposes next-token spans and, at each step, gates only the most critical pages from pre-encoded per-document caches, using query-conditioned page scoring and normalized-attention saliency; the verifier accepts spans and pages in an overlapped pipeline, expanding the gate only on low-confidence cases. This merges sparse, per-step document selection with draft-and-verify so the large model rarely loads irrelevant caches, reducing latency and improving robustness to distractors. The design integrates sparse RAG selection, speculative RAG-style verification, and query-aware KV/page saliency to tightly couple retrieval budgeting with token acceptance.

result.text: The paper tackles the latency and compute blowup in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) caused by linearly increasing input length as more documents are retrieved. Its key insight is that most retrieved documents are irrelevant to each generation step, so encoding them in parallel and then sparsely selecting a small subset to attend to during autoregressive decoding can preserve quality while cutting computation. The proposed Sparse RAG encodes all retrieved documents independently into caches, prompts the LLM with special control tokens to assess and choose highly relevant caches on the fly, and then decodes by attending only to those selected caches, thereby merging per-document relevance assessment and generation into a single process. Empirical results on short- and long-form tasks show this sparse mechanism reduces the number of documents loaded during decoding, accelerating inference and often improving generation by filtering out distracting context.

args.text: We propose MoSA: Mixture-of-Shift Adaptation for unlabeled test-time streams that explicitly disentangles and schedules two update paths—label-prior reweighting and covariate adaptation—based on online evidence of the dominant shift. MoSA maintains streaming estimates of class priors via no-label label-shift learners while feeding a safe, small-step entropy–sharpness covariate update stabilized by per-layer BN interpolation and gated by OOD/gradient filters; a prediction-balanced reservoir breaks temporal correlations to make both estimators reliable. At each step, a tiny convex selector chooses mixture weights between prior reweighting and feature updates to minimize a proxy risk subject to stability constraints, preventing forgetting and collapse under small, non-i.i.d. batches. This unified controller should reduce regret versus single-mechanism TTA under mixed shifts and yields practical robustness across batch sizes and streaming conditions.

result.text: The paper addresses the gap between current LLM research—focused mainly on using given tools—and the agent-like capability to decide whether to use a tool and which one(s) to pick from a set to satisfy user requests. To quantify this, the authors introduce MetaTool, a benchmark and dataset called ToolE containing single- and multi-tool prompts, define tasks and four subtasks for selection evaluation, and evaluate eight popular LLMs to reveal performance gaps and error modes. Based on results and analysis, they offer practical guidance—notably that tool developers should tailor description rewrites to the downstream LLM—to help improve tool-selection behavior.

result.text: We propose Counterfactual-Grounded Contrastive Decoding (CGCD) for LVLMs, which unifies token-level causal visual grounding with internal-activation trust signals to suppress object hallucinations at test time. At each decoding step, CGCD estimates a causal grounding score for candidate object/attribute tokens by grouping visual tokens into regions and measuring logit deltas under region-masking counterfactuals, then fuses this with sharpness/consistency statistics from hidden states to quantify hallucination risk. The risk adaptively subtracts penalties from candidate logits and guides a global beam re-ranking pass, while a lightweight co-occurrence prior only penalizes late, low-grounding mentions to avoid hurting fluency. This plug-and-play procedure amortizes cost via grouped perturbations and early token pruning, and is expected to outperform SID/HALC/LURE by only suppressing prior-driven tokens when internal evidence indicates ungroundedness.

result.text: We propose an identifiability algebra for object-centric multi-view causal representation learning under occlusion: when each view reveals only a subset of objects, the co-visibility hypergraph across views and scenes can guarantee recovery of object-wise causal latents up to per-slot reparameterizations. Concretely, under a compositional-and-irreducible object generative process and smooth view-dependent mixing, identifiability holds if (i) the co-visibility hypergraph is pairwise-connected (every slot chain-co-occurs across some sequence of view subsets) and (ii) each slot experiences at least one sparse, slot-targeted perturbation across the dataset—or, alternatively, instance-dependent sparsity of slot visibility provides sufficient support variation. We instantiate this with a contrastive, multi-view slot encoder that enforces cycle-consistent slot matching on the co-visibility graph and a causal-loss that anchors which slot changed under interventions, yielding stronger guarantees and fewer required perturbations than monolithic encoders. This unifies multi-view partial-observability, object-centric structure, and sparsity/interventions into a single theoretical and algorithmic framework.

The key insight is to split retrieval evidence across multiple lightweight drafts produced in parallel by a smaller, distilled specialist model and then have a single, larger generalist model verify and reconcile those drafts, which both increases evidence diversity and reduces per-draft context length and position bias. args.text: Contingency-Aware Planning (CAP) builds fallback-aware execution graphs for LLM tool agents, selecting both primary and contingency toolchains to bound tail risk and budget overruns. It learns calibrated per-step failure and latency distributions by fusing emulator-simulated outcomes with on-policy traces, then solves a constrained stochastic planning problem to allocate minimal-cost k-alternative branches and trigger policies. At runtime, before high-risk or ambiguous invocations, CAP injects contrastive, tool-specific clarifications and enables rapid intra-toolkit substitution when early anomaly signals fire. Evaluated with stepwise progress and failure-severity metrics on realistic tool tasks, CAP aims to reduce catastrophic dead-ends with modest overhead while producing actionable diagnostics for tool designers.

result.text: The paper tackles the fundamental ill-posedness of Causal Representation Learning (CRL), which aims to recover hidden causal variables and their relations from observational data but typically requires strong assumptions like temporal structure, interventions, or supervision to be identifiable. Its key insight is that identifiability can instead be achieved via a weak structural constraint on the observed mixing: observational variables can be partitioned into groups that each depend on only a subset of latent causal factors, and this grouping suffices to pin down the latent causal representation without temporal or interventional information. Methodologically, the authors formalize a generative model with grouped observational variables, derive identifiability results under these grouping conditions, and propose a self-supervised estimation framework tailored to the model; they prove statistical consistency and empirically demonstrate improved CRL performance and robustness to latent confounders and cycles compared to prior methods.

result.text: The paper addresses how to design caching algorithms in the learning-augmented framework that perform near-optimally with accurate predictions while retaining worst-case guarantees, but with the additional constraint that only a limited (sublinear) number of predictions can be queried. The key insight is that one can obtain the same quantitative trade-offs between consistency (performance when predictions are good) and robustness (worst-case guarantees) as prior work while dramatically reducing reliance on predictions by strategically querying them only when most beneficial. Methodologically, the authors develop caching algorithms that selectively request predictions for a sublinear subset of requests and combine these sparse predictions with classical online eviction rules and competitive analysis to prove bounds on consistency and robustness comparable to full-prediction algorithms. Their results show that parsimonious use of predictions suffices to reach the same asymptotic performance guarantees as algorithms that use predictions for every request.

result.text: The paper addresses slow and sometimes brittle inference in pretrained language models by enabling dynamic early stopping to save computation while maintaining or improving accuracy. The key insight is that attaching simple internal classifiers to each layer and stopping when their predictions stop changing for a fixed number of consecutive layers (a “patience” threshold) prevents overthinking and unnecessary deeper computation. The method—Patience-based Early Exit—therefore runs the model sequentially, checks intermediate predictions at each layer, and halts inference once the same class is predicted for a preset number of steps, yielding fewer average layers evaluated; experiments with ALBERT show this plug-and-play approach improves efficiency and robustness and gives a better accuracy-speed trade-off than prior early-exit strategies.

Under high uncertainty, lower temperature widens activation to multiple experts and applies mutual-distillation among co-activated experts to avoid narrow vision; under low uncertainty, sharpen routing and enforce orthogonalized expert representations to preserve specialization and reduce interference. When persistent disagreement clusters emerge, optionally spawn specialists initialized from the MoE subspace and distill them back into the MoE to scalably add capacity without destabilizing training. This fuses uncertainty-aware conditioning, MoE scaling, and diversity-preserving regularization to improve zero-shot generalization on procedurally diverse benchmarks.

result.text: We propose MoSA: Mixture-of-Shift Adaptation for unlabeled test-time streams that explicitly disentangles and schedules two update paths—label-prior reweighting and covariate adaptation—based on online evidence of the dominant shift. MoSA maintains streaming estimates of class priors via no-label label-shift learners while feeding a safe, small-step entropy–sharpness covariate update stabilized by per-layer BN interpolation and gated by OOD/gradient filters; a prediction-balanced reservoir breaks temporal correlations to make both estimators reliable. At each step, a tiny convex selector chooses mixture weights between prior reweighting and feature updates to minimize a proxy risk subject to stability constraints, preventing forgetting and collapse under small, non-i.i.d. batches. This unified controller should reduce regret versus single-mechanism TTA under mixed shifts and yields practical robustness across batch sizes and streaming conditions.

result.text: Contingency-Aware Planning (CAP) builds fallback-aware execution graphs for LLM tool agents, selecting both primary and contingency toolchains to bound tail risk and budget overruns. It learns calibrated per-step failure and latency distributions by fusing emulator-simulated outcomes with on-policy traces, then solves a constrained stochastic planning problem to allocate minimal-cost k-alternative branches and trigger policies. At runtime, before high-risk or ambiguous invocations, CAP injects contrastive, tool-specific clarifications and enables rapid intra-toolkit substitution when early anomaly signals fire. Evaluated with stepwise progress and failure-severity metrics on realistic tool tasks, CAP aims to reduce catastrophic dead-ends with modest overhead while producing actionable diagnostics for tool designers.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of detecting knowledge hallucinations in LLM outputs, arguing that current token-level uncertainty or text-level self-consistency methods lose rich semantic information during decoding. Its key insight is that dense internal activations of LLMs retain semantic structure useful for judging response consistency, so analyzing these representations can better reveal hallucinations than post-decoding signals. The authors introduce INSIDE, which computes an EigenScore by measuring eigenvalues of the covariance matrix of response embeddings to quantify semantic consistency/diversity, and propose a test-time feature clipping technique that truncates extreme internal activations to reduce overconfident, hallucinated generations. They validate these methods with extensive experiments and ablations across multiple LLMs and QA benchmarks, showing improved hallucination detection performance.

During training, we impose interchange-equivalence constraints on individual latents and use gradient-based edge pruning to identify the minimal edge set mediating each latent’s effect, yielding compact, faithful per-feature circuits with reduced polysemanticity and edit-ready structure. We will evaluate on GPT-2-small’s IOI and the greater-than mechanism, and use an automated interpretability agent to propose counterfactual prompts and targeted variable swaps for systematic testing. We hypothesize IC-SFC improves intervention minimality, compositionality, and transfer across prompts compared to standard SAEs or unconstrained circuit discovery.

result.text: We propose identifiable object-centric multi-view causal representation learning under occlusion and unlabeled sparse interventions. Each view observes a nonlinear mixture of a subset of objects, and episodes provide pre/post pairs where a single object property is perturbed but the object identity and affected view(s) are unknown. By combining object-level compositional irreducibility with the multi-view identifiability algebra, we show the object latents and cross-view correspondences are uniquely recoverable (up to permutation) when each object is visible in at least two views across episodes and receives occasional perturbations; we instantiate this with contrastively aligned slot encoders whose slots predict which views registered the change. This reduces supervision relative to labeled interventions and improves sample efficiency under heavy occlusion versus monolithic encoders.

result.text: The paper tackles the open problem of mechanistically explaining how a real-world language model accomplishes a nontrivial linguistic task—indirect object identification (IOI)—rather than toy behaviors or only high-level descriptions of large models. Its key insight is that GPT-2 small performs IOI via a distributed but tractable “circuit” composed of 26 attention heads that cluster into seven functional classes whose causal roles can be probed and characterized. Methodologically, the authors combine multiple interpretability tools—notably causal interventions, ablations, and quantitative metrics for faithfulness, completeness, and minimality—to identify, group, and validate these heads’ contributions to IOI and to measure how well the proposed circuit explains model behavior. The results show a largely faithful, reasonably complete, and compact explanation while highlighting residual gaps, arguing that mechanistic reverse-engineering of realistic language-model behaviors is feasible and scalable.
