result.text: We propose Retrieval-Amortized Test-Time Adaptation (RATTA): instead of performing per-neighbor gradient updates at inference, a small hypernetwork maps a query plus its retrieved examples to per-layer low‑rank adapter weights and an instance‑specific early‑exit policy, enabling fast, gradient‑free conditioning. The hypernetwork is trained to distill the effect of gradient-based test-time training on retrieved neighbors, while also learning to route or compose from a library of reusable adapters for further efficiency. At inference, the frozen base LM is modulated by the generated adapters, and a patience-calibrated exit head halts computation on easy inputs, preserving most of the gains of retrieval TTT at a fraction of the latency. This combines the accuracy benefits of retrieval-driven adaptation with amortized modulation and adapter reuse to yield scalable, compute‑aware online adaptation.

result.text: We propose identifiable object-centric multi-view causal representation learning under occlusion and unlabeled sparse interventions. Each view observes a nonlinear mixture of a subset of objects, and episodes provide pre/post pairs where a single object property is perturbed but the object identity and affected view(s) are unknown. By combining object-level compositional irreducibility with the multi-view identifiability algebra, we show the object latents and cross-view correspondences are uniquely recoverable (up to permutation) when each object is visible in at least two views across episodes and receives occasional perturbations; we instantiate this with contrastively aligned slot encoders whose slots predict which views registered the change. This reduces supervision relative to labeled interventions and improves sample efficiency under heavy occlusion versus monolithic encoders.

The key insight is that such routed models obey generalized power-law scaling laws that depend on both parameter count and compute, allowing a unified description that reduces to standard scaling for dense models and captures behavior across many routing architectures and training methods. The authors derive these two-variable scaling laws theoretically and validate them empirically across five orders of magnitude and three routing techniques, then define an Effective Parameter Count that collapses models onto a single scaling curve and use the fitted coefficients to quantitatively compare routing methods. result.text: The paper studies the “modality gap,” a geometric phenomenon where different data modalities (e.g., images and text) occupy distinct, arm’s-length regions in the shared embedding space of multi-modal contrastive models like CLIP, which can hinder downstream performance and fairness. The key insight is that this gap arises from two interacting causes: (1) standard neural network initialization biases each encoder’s outputs into a narrow cone so that different encoders start separated, and (2) contrastive optimization—particularly the temperature hyperparameter—preserves or enforces a nonzero separation between modalities during training. To analyze and mitigate this, the authors combine empirical measurement and theoretical analysis of initialization-induced concentration with controlled contrastive training experiments that vary temperature and alignment forces, showing that adjusting the modality gap can substantially affect zero-shot classification accuracy and fairness outcomes.

result.text: We propose an identifiability algebra for object-centric multi-view causal representation learning under occlusion: when each view reveals only a subset of objects, the co-visibility hypergraph across views and scenes can guarantee recovery of object-wise causal latents up to per-slot reparameterizations. Concretely, under a compositional-and-irreducible object generative process and smooth view-dependent mixing, identifiability holds if (i) the co-visibility hypergraph is pairwise-connected (every slot chain-co-occurs across some sequence of view subsets) and (ii) each slot experiences at least one sparse, slot-targeted perturbation across the dataset—or, alternatively, instance-dependent sparsity of slot visibility provides sufficient support variation. We instantiate this with a contrastive, multi-view slot encoder that enforces cycle-consistent slot matching on the co-visibility graph and a causal-loss that anchors which slot changed under interventions, yielding stronger guarantees and fewer required perturbations than monolithic encoders. This unifies multi-view partial-observability, object-centric structure, and sparsity/interventions into a single theoretical and algorithmic framework.

result.text: The paper tackles the vulnerability of test-time adaptation (TTA) methods to noisy, unexpected samples in unlabeled test streams—scenarios like unseen objects or corrupted inputs where existing TTA algorithms can be misled by blindly adapting to every incoming example. The key insight is that robustness requires screening out harmful inputs and stabilizing parameter updates: selectively adapting on high-confidence, class-uniform samples reduces the influence of outliers, while minimizing an entropy-sharpness objective guards parameters against destabilizing large gradients. result.text: The paper tackles object hallucination in large vision-language models (LVLMs), where models describe objects that are not present in images, undermining tasks like visual summarization and reasoning. The key insight is that hallucination arises from predictable statistical factors—object co-occurrence patterns, decoder uncertainty, and a tendency for hallucinated items to appear later in generated text—which can be exploited post-hoc to reduce false mentions. The authors propose LURE (LVLM Hallucination Revisor), a model-agnostic, post-processing algorithm that re-scores and reconstructs generated descriptions by accounting for co-occurrence priors, uncertainty signals, and positional cues to suppress unlikely objects. Evaluated on six open-source LVLMs, LURE yields about a 23% improvement on object-hallucination metrics and ranks highest in both GPT and human evaluations.

result.text: We propose object-centric causal representation learning under multi-view partial observability with environment-wise sparse interventions viewed as compressed-sensing codes over slots. Building on identifiability from shared multi-view structure, instance-dependent sparsity in mixing/observability, and compositional object factors, we show that if the view-by-environment intervention/masking design satisfies a simple cover/RIP-like condition, then object-level causal variables and their interventional effects are identifiable up to slot permutation. We instantiate this with a slot-contrastive multi-view encoder that uses environment-indexed FiLM and group-lasso regularization to match interventional signatures across views, leveraging environment-driven parameter changes in polynomial SEMs to estimate mechanisms. Compared to prior object-centric sparse-perturbation methods, this removes the need for labeled targets or full visibility and predicts identifiability per slot via a combinatorial algebra over the view-environment design.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of reliably identifying functionally important features in neural networks, noting that conventional sparse autoencoders (SAEs) often capture dataset structure rather than directions crucial to the network’s computation. The key insight is to train the sparse dictionary end-to-end so that the learned sparse codes are constrained to preserve the original model’s output distribution—measured by minimizing the KL divergence between outputs of the intact model and the model with SAE-reconstructed activations—thereby forcing the dictionary to capture features that are actually functionally relevant. Methodologically, they augment SAE training with this KL objective and compare e2e SAEs to standard SAEs, showing Pareto improvements: e2e features explain more of network performance, use fewer total features, and require fewer active features per example while retaining interpretability, and they release code for reproducing the experiments.

result.text: We propose Retrieval-Amortized Test-Time Adaptation (RATTA): instead of performing per-neighbor gradient updates at inference, a small hypernetwork maps a query plus its retrieved examples to per-layer low‑rank adapter weights and an instance‑specific early‑exit policy, enabling fast, gradient‑free conditioning. The hypernetwork is trained to distill the effect of gradient-based test-time training on retrieved neighbors, while also learning to route or compose from a library of reusable adapters for further efficiency. At inference, the frozen base LM is modulated by the generated adapters, and a patience-calibrated exit head halts computation on easy inputs, preserving most of the gains of retrieval TTT at a fraction of the latency. This combines the accuracy benefits of retrieval-driven adaptation with amortized modulation and adapter reuse to yield scalable, compute‑aware online adaptation.

result.text: The paper addresses the neglected problem of relationship hallucinations in large vision-language models (LVLMs), where models invent or misattribute relationships between objects despite object detection being largely solvable. Its key insight is that relationship hallucinations arise from specific co-occurrence biases—relationship-relationship, subject-relationship, and relationship-object—and from long-tail distributions in visual instruction tuning data that push models to over-rely on language priors rather than visual evidence. To quantify and analyze this, the authors introduce R-Bench, a benchmark comprising image-level and instance-level questions designed to probe existence and local comprehension of visual relationships, and use it to show that current LVLMs often ignore visual content, depend on commonsense LLM knowledge, and fail at contextual spatial reasoning. Their empirical analysis highlights dataset bias and model tendencies as primary drivers of relationship hallucination and points to the need for targeted data and evaluation to improve relational visual reasoning.

result.text: The paper addresses how to inject known causal structure into neural networks so they remain data-driven while becoming more interpretable and aligned with domain knowledge. The key insight is to train networks to reproduce the counterfactual behavior of an explicit causal model by swapping (interchanging) aligned internal representations between a base and a source input, thereby enforcing that interventions in the causal model correspond to interventions in the neural model. Their method, interchange intervention training (IIT), aligns variables in a chosen causal model with neural representations and minimizes a differentiable loss that encourages the network’s outputs under swapped internal activations to match the causal model’s counterfactual outputs; when this loss reaches zero the causal model is a formal causal abstraction of the network. Experiments on vision, navigation-language, and NLI benchmarks show IIT outperforms multitask and augmentation baselines and yields models whose internal behavior more faithfully realizes the target causal structure.

result.text: The paper addresses hallucinations in large vision-language models (LVLMs), where generated text can diverge from image content, noting that existing visual contrastive decoding methods fail to reliably suppress hallucinatory tokens due to uncontrolled global visual uncertainty. The key insight is that contrastive decoding’s effectiveness depends on precisely amplifying the preference gap between hallucinated and target tokens, which can be achieved by replacing noisy global uncertainty signals with a learned, theoretically grounded preference model to more accurately identify and penalize hallucinatory outputs. The authors propose Hallucination-Induced Optimization (HIO), which fine-tunes a Contrary Bradley-Terry preference model to amplify contrasts between hallucinatory and correct tokens and then uses this model to guide contrastive decoding, thereby more effectively discouraging hallucinations. Experiments across multiple benchmarks show HIO reduces hallucinations and outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods.

result.text: The paper addresses unsupervised nonlinear disentanglement of latent factors in naturalistic videos, where prior methods rely on unrealistic assumptions that only a few factors change at any time and have been tested on synthetic datasets. Its key insight is that in segmented natural movies factor transitions are temporally sparse—mostly small changes with occasional large jumps—so enforcing sparsity in temporal changes can recover disentangled generative factors without knowing how many factors change. The authors introduce SlowVAE, a VAE-based model that imposes a sparse prior on differences between temporally adjacent latent representations, prove an identifiability result for this formulation, and empirically show it outperforms or matches state-of-the-art on benchmarks and transfers to more natural video datasets (Natural Sprites and KITTI Masks) that they propose for future disentanglement research.

args.text: We propose LA-KV: a learning-augmented, robust KV paging layer for long-context LLMs. A tiny predictor emits a one-bit hint per cache page at each step—"reuse within the next phase" vs. "safe to evict"—computed from normalized-attention surrogates (ZipCache-style) and recent query statistics; a Quest-like selector then loads only the hinted top-K while Ada-KV assigns per-head budgets. We import one-bit paging theory to craft an eviction/selection rule that is consistent under perfect hints yet preserves competitive worst-case guarantees under adversarial hints, and we add a small recurrent summary (LESS) so mistaken evictions remain recoverable. This yields query-aware, theoretically grounded paging that cuts IO and latency without sacrificing long-range recall.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of circuit analysis in transformer language models, where densely activating MLP sublayers and features found by sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are spread across many nonlinear neurons, making circuits either intractably large or entangled. The key insight is that a densely activating MLP can be faithfully approximated by a wider, sparsely activating MLP—called a transcoder—whose sparse activations let weights-based circuit analysis disentangle input-dependent from input-invariant contributions. The authors introduce a method to train transcoders to mimic original MLP layers while imposing sparsity, show that these transcoders match or exceed SAEs on sparsity, faithfulness, and interpretability across models from 120M to 1.4B parameters, and demonstrate their utility by reverse-engineering and gaining new insights into the “greater-than” circuit in GPT2-small.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of optimizing reinforcement learning policies to maximally satisfy Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) specifications, where standard RL’s myopic reward-based learning struggles to find policies with highest long-run satisfaction probability. The key insight is that by introducing an “eventual discounting” value-function proxy one can align value-based optimization with maximizing the probability of satisfying LTL formulas, and that additional learning signal can be obtained by imagining alternate futures in which different satisfaction paths occurred. Methodologically, the authors define an eventual discounting objective and derive corresponding value estimates, then introduce a counterfactual experience replay mechanism that synthesizes off-policy training transitions from on-policy rollouts via reasoning about other ways the LTL goal could have been achieved, and they validate this approach empirically in both discrete and continuous domains.

The key insight is that object-centric inductive biases restore identifiability because representing each object with its own slot makes the generative mapping effectively injective over object properties, so sparse perturbations targeted to objects provide much stronger supervision for causal disentanglement than global Euclidean encodings. Methodologically, the authors modify the Slot Attention architecture to produce object-wise representations and train it with weak supervision from sparse interventions (perturbations) so that each slot learns disentangled properties; empirically this object-centric approach disentangles object attributes with far fewer perturbations than a comparable monolithic encoder in image-based experiments.

Its key insight is that many LoRAs share structure and can be jointly compressed into a common low-rank basis plus small adapter-specific scaling matrices, and that grouping similar LoRAs into clusters enables scalable joint compression. result.text: The paper addresses why reinforcement learning agents often fail to generalize from limited training environments to unseen test conditions, arguing that the sequential decision-making setting creates a distinct challenge not captured by supervised-learning generalization analysis. The key insight is that uncertainty about which training conditions will occur at test time induces implicit partial observability—turning nominally fully observed MDPs into “epistemic POMDPs” whose hidden state encodes epistemic uncertainty about environment parameters. The authors formalize this epistemic POMDP and show that methods ignoring the induced partial observability fail, then propose a simple ensemble-based approach that approximates inference over the hidden epistemic state and thereby better conditions policies on uncertainty. Empirically, their ensemble-derived method significantly improves generalization on Procgen compared to baselines, supporting the view that RL generalization requires explicitly addressing epistemic partial observability.

result.text: The paper addresses the need for calibrated uncertainty estimates from learned trajectory (diffusion) dynamics models used for planning in uncertain, dynamic, and partially observable robotic environments. The key insight is to apply Conformal Prediction (CP) to diffusion-based trajectory predictors: by using a finite exchangeable calibration set to produce coverage regions in trajectory space with guaranteed probability, and by incorporating a quantile-based loss during training to make the diffusion model’s outputs more amenable to calibration. Their method, PlanCP, modifies the diffusion model’s loss to include a quantile term that encourages robustness across examples, then uses a conformal calibration step at test time to produce trajectory coverage sets at a user-specified coverage level; these sets are used within planning and offline model-based RL to reduce uncertainty and improve performance. result.text: The paper addresses the problem of slow inference for long-context large language models, where self-attention becomes bottlenecked by loading a large key-value (KV) cache as sequence length grows. The key insight is that only a small subset of KV cache tokens are critical for a particular query and that token criticality depends on the query vector, so one can predict which cache pages matter without scanning the whole cache. They propose Quest, a query-aware KV cache page selection algorithm that maintains min/max key summaries per cache page and uses the query to estimate page criticality, loading only the top-K pages for attention; this approach yields large self-attention and end-to-end latency speedups (up to 2.23x and 7.03x respectively) with negligible accuracy loss on long-dependency tasks.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of recurrent neural network (RNN) world model backbones in model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL), namely their limited long-term memory when simulating future observations in partially observable environments. Its key insight is that alternative sequence models—Transformers and Structured State Space (S4) models—offer complementary strengths for capturing long-range dependencies, and that S4 in particular can provide superior long-term memory and efficiency for latent imagination. The authors introduce S4WM, the first S4-based world model capable of generating high-dimensional image sequences via latent rollout, and perform extensive comparisons of RNN-, Transformer-, and S4-based world models on specially designed benchmarks testing long-term imagination, context-dependent recall, reward prediction, and memory-based reasoning. Empirically, S4WM outperforms Transformer-based world models on long-horizon memory tasks while requiring less computation during training and imagination, suggesting S4 is a promising backbone for stronger MBRL agents.

result.text: The paper tackles task-agnostic continual online reinforcement learning where an agent must continually solve unseen, nonstationary tasks from streaming data without access to task labels, pretraining on a known task distribution, or clear task boundaries. Its key insight is to model changing dynamics as an infinite mixture of Gaussian Process experts, so the system can both flexibly create new dynamics models when novel regimes appear and efficiently reuse existing ones while quantifying uncertainty for model-based planning. Methodologically, the authors maintain a mixture-of-experts dynamics model with each expert implemented as a Gaussian Process, introduce a temporal transition prior to capture dependencies in the data stream, and update the mixture online via sequential variational inference so new components can be spawned or old ones reactivated; this model-based RL pipeline is then used for planning and demonstrated to outperform baselines on nonstationary control and driving tasks.

result.text: The paper addresses object hallucination in grounded image captioning, where models produce words not supported by the visual scene due to misclassification or reliance on language priors. Its key insight is that aligning structural semantic information across modalities — i.e., enforcing consensus between a visual graph (scene graph) and a language graph that capture nodes and their relations — reduces semantic inconsistency and thus hallucination. The proposed Consensus Graph Representation Learning (CGRL) framework learns this cross-modal consensus representation by explicitly aligning nodes and edges of the visual and language graphs and injecting the aligned consensus into the grounded captioning pipeline so the model better captures both linguistic characteristics and visual relevance, then grounds generated object words to image regions. Experiments on Flickr30k Entities show CGRL substantially reduces hallucination (−9% CHAIRi) while improving captioning and grounding metrics (+2.9 CIDEr, +2.3 F1LOC) and human-evaluated quality.

result.text: The paper addresses the tendency of large sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models to overfit and suffer from sparse, imbalanced data allocation as the expert count grows, which caps performance especially on limited-data tasks. The key insight is that routing should encourage variance-aware, cluster-level diversity among experts so that experts learn more distinct and appropriate knowledge rather than redundant or undertrained behaviors. The authors propose Mixture of Expert Clusters (MoEC), which groups experts into clusters and imposes variance-based constraints during routing to promote balanced activation and diversity, together with a cluster-level expert dropout mechanism tailored to the clustered structure. Empirical results on machine translation and NLU show that MoEC mitigates overfitting and sparse allocation, unlocking better performance from large-scale sparse models.

result.text: The paper addresses when and how unsupervised object-centric representations can be learned provably from visual scenes, filling a theoretical gap behind empirically successful methods. Its key insight is that if the scene generation satisfies two properties—compositionality (the scene is generated by composing object-specific factors) and irreducibility (object factors cannot be further decomposed)—then the true object representations are identifiable even when objects are dependent. The authors prove that an inference model that is both invertible and compositional recovers the ground-truth object factors under this generative model, validate the theory on synthetic datasets, and show that existing object-centric methods’ empirical identifiability correlates with their measured compositionality and invertibility.

result.text: The paper addresses the limited expressiveness of Neural Processes (NPs), whose reliance on a single global latent variable hinders modeling complex, multimodal data-generating processes and restricts their applicability in meta-learning and few-shot settings. Its key insight is that augmenting NPs with a mixture-of-experts mechanism yields a richer, more flexible meta-representation by allowing multiple specialized latent components to capture diverse modes and local structure across tasks while preserving exchangeability. The method, Mixture of Expert Neural Processes (MoE-NPs), integrates a gating network and multiple expert NPs so that for each context the model infers a mixture over expert latents and aggregates expert predictions to produce task-conditional outputs; this architecture is trained end-to-end and applied to few-shot supervised and meta-reinforcement learning benchmarks, where it shows improved generalization to unseen tasks.

result.text: The paper addresses the persistent problem of object hallucinations in large vision-language models (LVLMs), where models generate visually inconsistent or non-existent object references. The key insight is that hallucinations can be reduced by jointly leveraging fine-grained local grounding to correct tokens as they are produced and a global search strategy to favor grounded hypotheses during sequence decoding. HALC implements this by adding an auto-focal grounding mechanism that dynamically assesses and rectifies token-level visual alignment, combined with a specialized beam-search decoding that re-ranks beams based on grounding consistency, and it operates as a plug-and-play decoding module requiring no additional training. Experimental results across four benchmarks show that this dual local–global approach lowers object hallucinations while maintaining generation quality, outperforming prior methods.

result.text: The paper tackles the slowdown and huge memory use of self-attention on long sequences by addressing not just algorithmic complexity but IO between GPU memory levels. The key insight is that attention implementations should be IO-aware: by tiling computations to keep working sets in fast on-chip SRAM and minimize reads/writes to slower high-bandwidth memory, one can perform exact attention with far fewer memory accesses and near-optimal IO complexity for practical SRAM sizes. The authors implement FlashAttention, an IO-aware tiled attention kernel (and a block-sparse variant) that computes exact attention while streaming tiles through on-chip memory to avoid materializing large intermediate matrices, and they demonstrate large real-world speedups (e.g., 15% on BERT-large, 3× on GPT-2 for 1K seqs) and improved quality/long-context capabilities on long-sequence tasks.

Its key insight is to cast circuit discovery as a continuous optimization problem and apply gradient-based pruning not to neurons or modules but to the edges between components, which yields much sparser and more faithful circuits. Its key insight is that user-provided advice—formalized as potentially partial, fragmented, or imperfect deterministic finite automata (DFAs)—can be incorporated to guide learning and speed up discovery of the hidden reward structure without requiring the reward function to be fully specified. result.text: The paper tackles causal representation learning when observations are only partially informative—each measurement reveals a subset of latent causal variables and the observable subset can vary per instance—challenging standard identifiability assumptions that all latents are always reflected in data. The key insight is that an instance-dependent sparsity pattern in how latents mix into observations provides a principled constraint that enables identifiability: under either linear mixing with minimal assumptions or piecewise-linear mixing with Gaussian latents, the true causal factors can be recovered. Methodologically, the authors derive two theoretical identifiability results and develop two corresponding estimation algorithms that encourage sparsity in the recovered representations to match the partial-observability structure. result.text: We propose Counterfactual Activation Sharpness (CAS) decoding for LVLMs: a training-free, test-time method that penalizes tokens whose likelihood is fragile to targeted visual perturbations but stable to text paraphrases. CAS builds counterfactual mini-batches by selectively pruning unimportant vision tokens early in the network and by paraphrasing the prefix; for each candidate next token it estimates a Hallucination Fragility Score as the variance of token logits across visual counterfactuals minus that across text counterfactuals, normalized by an internal-activation sharpness/consistency measure. This score is then used to reweight logits during decoding—optionally combined with a lightweight preference model—thereby suppressing visually ungrounded continuations while preserving instruction consistency. By unifying introspective token selection with internal-representation diagnostics and principled contrastive reweighting, CAS targets object and attribute hallucinations with minimal overhead and without extra data.

We formalize dataset design as maximizing a submodular surrogate combining (i) pairwise-connectedness and cycle-basis coverage of the co-visibility hypergraph and (ii) a restricted-isometry proxy of the slot-by-environment intervention/masking matrix, which together guarantee object-wise identifiability under compositional irreducibility and smooth mixing. result.text: The paper addresses the memory bottleneck caused by the KV cache during autoregressive inference of large language models, which can exceed model weight size and limit throughput due to constrained batch sizes. The key insight is the "persistence of importance" hypothesis: tokens that exerted large attention influence at one generation step are likely to remain influential in future steps, so retaining a small subset of pivotal KV entries suffices for high-quality generation. The authors present Scissorhands, a test-time, model-agnostic KV cache management system that probabilistically retains and stores pivotal tokens (based on empirical and theoretical analysis of attention scores) to enforce a fixed memory budget without finetuning, achieving up to 5× KV memory reduction and, when combined with 4-bit weight quantization, up to 20× total compression with minimal quality loss.

result.text: We propose an identifiability algebra for object-centric multi-view causal representation learning under occlusion: when each view reveals only a subset of objects, the co-visibility hypergraph across views and scenes can guarantee recovery of object-wise causal latents up to per-slot reparameterizations. Concretely, under a compositional-and-irreducible object generative process and smooth view-dependent mixing, identifiability holds if (i) the co-visibility hypergraph is pairwise-connected (every slot chain-co-occurs across some sequence of view subsets) and (ii) each slot experiences at least one sparse, slot-targeted perturbation across the dataset—or, alternatively, instance-dependent sparsity of slot visibility provides sufficient support variation. We instantiate this with a contrastive, multi-view slot encoder that enforces cycle-consistent slot matching on the co-visibility graph and a causal-loss that anchors which slot changed under interventions, yielding stronger guarantees and fewer required perturbations than monolithic encoders. This unifies multi-view partial-observability, object-centric structure, and sparsity/interventions into a single theoretical and algorithmic framework.

args.text: Risk-Budgeted Contingency Trees (RBCT) allocate and enforce a global tail-risk budget across an LLM agent’s branched tool-execution plan. RBCT first samples diverse plan trees, fits per-step failure/latency models with emulator traces, and wraps them in split-conformal bounds to yield calibrated step risk; it then solves a chance/CVaR-constrained allocation to choose primary and fallback branches and to place low-cost probes or clarifications where their value-of-information most reduces budget consumption. During execution, a Lagrangian risk controller tracks realized outcomes and dynamically re-allocates remaining risk, enabling rapid intra-toolkit substitutions while maintaining plan-level α-violation control. On realistic multimodal, real-tool tasks, RBCT targets fewer catastrophic dead-ends and budget overruns versus stepwise-only or risk-neutral planners at comparable cost.

result.text: The paper tackles hallucinations in large vision-language models (LVLMs), where models generate incorrect or ungrounded text, without relying on costly extra data or doubling inference. Its key insight is that pretrained LVLMs can introspectively judge the importance of visual tokens conditioned on prior vision and text context, so selectively removing unimportant vision tokens early can amplify text-informed hallucination signals that reveal vision-text associations. The method, Self-Introspective Decoding (SID), uses a Context and Text-aware Token Selection (CT2S) strategy to prune unimportant vision tokens after early layers, computes amplified hallucination logits driven by the remaining vision-text association, and subtracts these from the original token logits during autoregressive decoding to suppress aimless visual hallucinations. Experiments show SID reduces hallucinations and improves text quality across metrics without extra knowledge sources and with minimal added computation.

The key insight is to use the model’s own detailed, self-generated descriptions of the image as contrastive references: comparing candidate continuations against those descriptions helps identify and suppress tokens that deviate from the actual visual content. The method, COuntering DEscription Contrastive Decoding (CODE), computes token-level adjustments during decoding by dynamically reweighting next-token probabilities based on similarity to the self-generated description versus the primary prompt-conditioned distribution, thereby steering generation toward outputs aligned with the visual counterpart. CODE is a plug-in contrastive decoding strategy that requires no extra training and empirically reduces hallucinations and improves cross-modal consistency across multiple benchmarks.

result.text: The paper tackles the latency and compute blowup in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) caused by linearly increasing input length as more documents are retrieved. Its key insight is that most retrieved documents are irrelevant to each generation step, so encoding them in parallel and then sparsely selecting a small subset to attend to during autoregressive decoding can preserve quality while cutting computation. The proposed Sparse RAG encodes all retrieved documents independently into caches, prompts the LLM with special control tokens to assess and choose highly relevant caches on the fly, and then decodes by attending only to those selected caches, thereby merging per-document relevance assessment and generation into a single process. Empirical results on short- and long-form tasks show this sparse mechanism reduces the number of documents loaded during decoding, accelerating inference and often improving generation by filtering out distracting context.

result.text: We propose ULTRA: an uncertainty‑calibrated latent temporal reward monitor that compiles natural‑language or LTL task specifications into executable automata operating directly on a learned world‑model latent space, providing dense, cheap feedback during imagination. Concretely, we align language and vision to the generative latent space (GenRL‑style grounding while mitigating the modality gap) and learn a dictionary of atomic propositions as lightweight latent classifiers with NML‑style calibrated uncertainty; these are then compiled (à la spec‑to‑reward) into differentiable automata that run each latent rollout step. During imagination we use the automata outputs as shaped rewards plus an intrinsic bonus from classifier uncertainty, and augment training with counterfactual satisfaction rollouts and an eventual‑discounting objective to maximize long‑run satisfaction probability. result.text: We propose identifiable object-centric multi-view causal representation learning under occlusion and unlabeled sparse interventions. Each view observes a nonlinear mixture of a subset of objects, and episodes provide pre/post pairs where a single object property is perturbed but the object identity and affected view(s) are unknown. By combining object-level compositional irreducibility with the multi-view identifiability algebra, we show the object latents and cross-view correspondences are uniquely recoverable (up to permutation) when each object is visible in at least two views across episodes and receives occasional perturbations; we instantiate this with contrastively aligned slot encoders whose slots predict which views registered the change. This reduces supervision relative to labeled interventions and improves sample efficiency under heavy occlusion versus monolithic encoders.

result.text: The paper addresses how to design caching algorithms in the learning-augmented framework that perform near-optimally with accurate predictions while retaining worst-case guarantees, but with the additional constraint that only a limited (sublinear) number of predictions can be queried. The key insight is that one can obtain the same quantitative trade-offs between consistency (performance when predictions are good) and robustness (worst-case guarantees) as prior work while dramatically reducing reliance on predictions by strategically querying them only when most beneficial. Methodologically, the authors develop caching algorithms that selectively request predictions for a sublinear subset of requests and combine these sparse predictions with classical online eviction rules and competitive analysis to prove bounds on consistency and robustness comparable to full-prediction algorithms. Their results show that parsimonious use of predictions suffices to reach the same asymptotic performance guarantees as algorithms that use predictions for every request.

result.text: The paper addresses how to predict and compare the performance of routed (conditional computation) language models, which use only subsets of parameters per input and thus introduce two independent scaling axes: total parameter count and compute per token. The key insight is that such routed models obey generalized power-law scaling laws that depend on both parameter count and compute, allowing a unified description that reduces to standard scaling for dense models and captures behavior across many routing architectures and training methods. The authors derive these two-variable scaling laws theoretically and validate them empirically across five orders of magnitude and three routing techniques, then define an Effective Parameter Count that collapses models onto a single scaling curve and use the fitted coefficients to quantitatively compare routing methods. This framework enables principled trade-offs and comparisons between model size, compute budget, and routing strategy for conditional computation architectures.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of building generalist embodied agents that can follow language or visual task specifications across diverse domains without task-specific reward engineering or large annotated multimodal datasets. Its key insight is to align representations from pretrained vision-language foundation models (VLMs) with the latent space of generative world models for reinforcement learning, enabling task grounding in embodied dynamics without any language annotations. The proposed method, GenRL, trains multimodal-foundation world models that map vision and/or language prompts into the world-model latent space and then trains policies “in imagination” using those latents, supplemented by a data-free policy learning strategy to bootstrap policy learning without extra environment data. Empirically, GenRL demonstrates multi-task generalization in large-scale locomotion and manipulation benchmarks, showing that VLM grounding into generative world models can enable prompt-driven behavior learning.

result.text: The paper addresses identifiability in multi-view representation learning when each view observes only a nonlinear mixture of a subset of underlying latent variables that may be causally related, i.e., the realistic partial-observability setting where prior full-observability identifiability results do not apply. The key insight is that shared information across all subsets of views suffices to recover the common latent factors up to a smooth bijection, and that simple graphical rules (an "identifiability algebra") can predict which specific latents are recoverable from which view combinations. Methodologically, the authors prove identifiability theorems showing contrastive learning with a single encoder per view can recover the shared latents, derive combinatorial/graphical criteria for variable-level identifiability, and validate the theory empirically on synthetic, image, and multimodal datasets, recovering prior methods as special cases.

result.text: Uncertainty-tempered MoE for RL generalization: train a soft Mixture-of-Experts policy/value whose router conditions on an ensemble-derived belief over latent environment parameters (epistemic POMDP) and dynamically adjusts its routing temperature by predictive disagreement. Under high uncertainty, lower temperature widens activation to multiple experts and applies mutual-distillation among co-activated experts to avoid narrow vision; under low uncertainty, sharpen routing and enforce orthogonalized expert representations to preserve specialization and reduce interference. When persistent disagreement clusters emerge, optionally spawn specialists initialized from the MoE subspace and distill them back into the MoE to scalably add capacity without destabilizing training. This fuses uncertainty-aware conditioning, MoE scaling, and diversity-preserving regularization to improve zero-shot generalization on procedurally diverse benchmarks.

args.text: We propose Conformal-Constrained Test-Time Adaptation (CoCo-TTA), an online wrapper that couples entropy-minimization with an explicit calibration-control constraint to maintain long-run coverage while improving accuracy under shift. A streaming conformal monitor tracks nonconformity quantiles on a small reservoir and updates a dual variable that jointly scales the adaptation step size and a trust-region penalty; updates are triggered by a martingale shift detector and applied only to low-entropy, diverse samples. The resulting primal–dual procedure minimizes marginal-entropy (or pseudo-label loss) subject to matching a target coverage/calibration profile, with rollback if reservoir coverage or an entropy–sharpness surrogate degrades. CoCo-TTA yields safe, selective adaptation that boosts accuracy under shift while preserving near-nominal calibration in the no-shift regime.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem that conventional value-based multi-agent RL methods, which use expected (risk-neutral) Q values under centralized training with decentralized execution, fail to coordinate reliably in stochastic and uncertain environments. The key insight is to optimize policies for risk-sensitive objectives by using Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) computed over learned return distributions for each agent, thereby prioritizing worst-case outcomes that improve coordination under uncertainty. RMIX learns per-agent return distributions and analytically computes decentralized CVaR estimates, introduces a dynamic risk-level predictor to adapt risk sensitivity over time, and trains end-to-end by using CVaR targets in the centralized TD error while using CVaR as an auxiliary local reward with quantile regression to update local distributional critics. Empirical results on challenging StarCraft II benchmarks show that RMIX yields better coordination and sample efficiency than state-of-the-art baselines.

result.text: We propose identifiable object-centric multi-view causal representation learning under occlusion and unlabeled sparse interventions. Each view observes a nonlinear mixture of a subset of objects, and episodes provide pre/post pairs where a single object property is perturbed but the object identity and affected view(s) are unknown. By combining object-level compositional irreducibility with the multi-view identifiability algebra, we show the object latents and cross-view correspondences are uniquely recoverable (up to permutation) when each object is visible in at least two views across episodes and receives occasional perturbations; we instantiate this with contrastively aligned slot encoders whose slots predict which views registered the change. This reduces supervision relative to labeled interventions and improves sample efficiency under heavy occlusion versus monolithic encoders.

result.text: Current query-aware KV paging reduces loads by scoring existing cache pages, but page boundaries are incidental to sequence order; as a result, attention mass is fragmented across many pages. We propose AttnPack, a learned KV cache layout that repacks keys/values into pagelets so that tokens frequently co-attended for real queries are co-located, using normalized-attention statistics and retrieval-time co-access to build a co-attention graph and solve a size-constrained partitioning. Plugged under Quest-style selectors and Sparse RAG’s per-document gating, AttnPack cuts page fan-out so top-K pages cover most saliency, while a tiny recurrent summary (LESS-style) shadows evicted clusters to preserve recoverability. This co-design of paging and layout targets large IO and latency reductions without retraining, and can be maintained incrementally for streaming inputs.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of improving language model performance with retrieval without incurring the training-vs.-inference mismatch and the quadratic cost in Transformer computation/memory from appending large retrieved contexts at test time. The key insight is that instead of concatenating retrieved neighbors to the input, one can fine-tune the model at test time on a small set of nearest-neighbor training examples using the model’s usual training procedure, which yields large gains even with very few gradient steps and neighbors. Concretely, the authors build a large distributed embedding index over the Pile, retrieve ~20 nearest neighbors per test input, and perform one gradient update per neighbor (test-time training) before evaluating, showing substantial improvements across 20+ language modeling tasks and dramatically closing the gap between small and much larger models, provided the retrieval index is sufficiently large and high-quality.

result.text: We propose an identifiability algebra for object-centric multi-view causal representation learning under occlusion: when each view reveals only a subset of objects, the co-visibility hypergraph across views and scenes can guarantee recovery of object-wise causal latents up to per-slot reparameterizations. Concretely, under a compositional-and-irreducible object generative process and smooth view-dependent mixing, identifiability holds if (i) the co-visibility hypergraph is pairwise-connected (every slot chain-co-occurs across some sequence of view subsets) and (ii) each slot experiences at least one sparse, slot-targeted perturbation across the dataset—or, alternatively, instance-dependent sparsity of slot visibility provides sufficient support variation. We instantiate this with a contrastive, multi-view slot encoder that enforces cycle-consistent slot matching on the co-visibility graph and a causal-loss that anchors which slot changed under interventions, yielding stronger guarantees and fewer required perturbations than monolithic encoders. This unifies multi-view partial-observability, object-centric structure, and sparsity/interventions into a single theoretical and algorithmic framework.

result.text: The paper addresses how to construct effective curricula for reinforcement learning by formally interpolating between an easy auxiliary (source) task distribution and a hard target distribution to enable gradual learning. Its key insight is to view curriculum generation as an optimal transport problem and to produce a sequence of intermediate task distributions along a geodesic (Wasserstein barycenter) between source and target, using a task-dependent contextual distance so shifts are small and meaningful. result.text: The paper tackles the vulnerability of test-time adaptation (TTA) methods to noisy, unexpected samples in unlabeled test streams—scenarios like unseen objects or corrupted inputs where existing TTA algorithms can be misled by blindly adapting to every incoming example. The key insight is that robustness requires screening out harmful inputs and stabilizing parameter updates: selectively adapting on high-confidence, class-uniform samples reduces the influence of outliers, while minimizing an entropy-sharpness objective guards parameters against destabilizing large gradients. The proposed method, SoTTA, implements input-wise robustness via high-confidence uniform-class sampling to filter test data and parameter-wise robustness through entropy-sharpness minimization during adaptation, and experiments on standard TTA benchmarks with various noisy conditions show SoTTA outperforms prior methods under noise while matching their accuracy on clean streams.

result.text: Contingency-Aware Planning (CAP) builds fallback-aware execution graphs for LLM tool agents, selecting both primary and contingency toolchains to bound tail risk and budget overruns. It learns calibrated per-step failure and latency distributions by fusing emulator-simulated outcomes with on-policy traces, then solves a constrained stochastic planning problem to allocate minimal-cost k-alternative branches and trigger policies. At runtime, before high-risk or ambiguous invocations, CAP injects contrastive, tool-specific clarifications and enables rapid intra-toolkit substitution when early anomaly signals fire. Evaluated with stepwise progress and failure-severity metrics on realistic tool tasks, CAP aims to reduce catastrophic dead-ends with modest overhead while producing actionable diagnostics for tool designers.

It builds unlabeled conformity scores from augmentation-marginal entropy and consistency, monitors their stream with a betting-martingale to detect shift, and maintains an online conformal acceptance band; a candidate parameter update is accepted only if it reduces the held-out reservoir’s conformal risk proxy, otherwise it is rolled back. result.text: The paper tackles object hallucination in large vision-language models (LVLMs), where models describe objects that are not present in images, undermining tasks like visual summarization and reasoning. The authors propose LURE (LVLM Hallucination Revisor), a model-agnostic, post-processing algorithm that re-scores and reconstructs generated descriptions by accounting for co-occurrence priors, uncertainty signals, and positional cues to suppress unlikely objects. Evaluated on six open-source LVLMs, LURE yields about a 23% improvement on object-hallucination metrics and ranks highest in both GPT and human evaluations.

result.text: We propose object-centric causal representation learning under multi-view partial observability with environment-wise sparse interventions viewed as compressed-sensing codes over slots. Building on identifiability from shared multi-view structure, instance-dependent sparsity in mixing/observability, and compositional object factors, we show that if the view-by-environment intervention/masking design satisfies a simple cover/RIP-like condition, then object-level causal variables and their interventional effects are identifiable up to slot permutation. We instantiate this with a slot-contrastive multi-view encoder that uses environment-indexed FiLM and group-lasso regularization to match interventional signatures across views, leveraging environment-driven parameter changes in polynomial SEMs to estimate mechanisms. Compared to prior object-centric sparse-perturbation methods, this removes the need for labeled targets or full visibility and predicts identifiability per slot via a combinatorial algebra over the view-environment design.

result.text: We propose ULTRA: an uncertainty‑calibrated latent temporal reward monitor that compiles natural‑language or LTL task specifications into executable automata operating directly on a learned world‑model latent space, providing dense, cheap feedback during imagination. Concretely, we align language and vision to the generative latent space (GenRL‑style grounding while mitigating the modality gap) and learn a dictionary of atomic propositions as lightweight latent classifiers with NML‑style calibrated uncertainty; these are then compiled (à la spec‑to‑reward) into differentiable automata that run each latent rollout step. During imagination we use the automata outputs as shaped rewards plus an intrinsic bonus from classifier uncertainty, and augment training with counterfactual satisfaction rollouts and an eventual‑discounting objective to maximize long‑run satisfaction probability. Using an S4‑based world model yields long‑horizon credit assignment and efficient monitoring, promising promptable generalists that learn from language without external reward queries.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of training policy-gradient RL agents that are robust to transition uncertainty in rectangular robust MDPs without incurring the high computational cost of existing robust methods. The key insight is that the worst-case transition kernel for rectangular uncertainty induces a worst-case state-action occupation measure that admits a closed-form expression and that the worst kernel is effectively a rank-one perturbation of the nominal kernel. Methodologically, the authors derive this closed-form worst occupation measure, combine it with a robust Q-value estimation to obtain an explicit robust policy gradient, and show that this robust policy gradient (RPG) can be estimated from data with the same time complexity as ordinary (non-robust) policy gradient algorithms, avoiding expensive convex optimization during training.

Its key insight is that normalized attention scores—adjusted to reflect the lower-triangle structure of autoregressive attention—provide a more accurate saliency metric than prior heuristics, and that a channel-separable tokenwise quantization scheme greatly reduces parameter overhead compared to fine-grained groupwise quantization. result.text: The paper tackles test-time adaptation for deployed, resource-constrained models (e.g., quantized, non-modifiable FPGAs) where conventional methods that require backpropagation and weight updates are infeasible. Its key insight is that adaptation can be achieved without changing model weights or computing gradients by optimizing an added input prompt and selectively shifting activations using a derivative-free evolution strategy guided by a fitness function combining test-vs-training statistic discrepancy and prediction entropy. The proposed method, FOA, uses covariance matrix adaptation to search for prompt vectors and an activation shifting scheme to align activations of shifted test samples to the source domain, enabling unsupervised online adaptation with only forward passes. Empirically, FOA runs on 8-bit quantized ViTs, outperforms gradient-based TENT on full-precision models, and dramatically reduces memory usage (up to 24×) on ImageNet-C.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of object hallucination in large vision-language models (LVLMs), extending scrutiny from single-class presence to how models misperceive and invent multiple distinct objects in realistic scenes. Its key insight is that LVLMs hallucinate more when required to recognize multiple objects simultaneously and that these errors are shaped by the distribution of object classes, salience, frequency, and dataset-induced shortcuts or spurious correlations. To quantify and analyze this phenomenon, the authors introduce ROPE (Recognition-based Object Probing Evaluation), an automated protocol that uses visual referring prompts and per-image class distributions to test multi-object recognition and reduce ambiguity. Through comprehensive empirical studies, they show systematic trends in multi-object hallucination and identify data- and model-specific factors that drive these failures, enabling more targeted mitigation strategies.

args.text: We propose hierarchical object–part causal representation learning under multi-view partial observability and occlusion, where each object is modeled as a tree-structured assembly of parts connected by kinematic constraints. We show that identifiability of part-wise causal latents and cross-view correspondences holds (up to per-part reparameterizations and tree automorphisms) if the part-level co-visibility hypergraph is pairwise-connected across episodes and either instance-dependent sparsity of part visibility provides sufficient support variation or occasional sparse, unlabeled joint-targeted perturbations occur. Algorithmically, we instantiate a multi-view slot-to-part encoder that enforces cycle-consistent matching on the part co-visibility graph and kinematic-cycle consistency on the tree, with a change-anchoring causal loss at the part level; an active designer selects next views and joint perturbations to close algebra-predicted identifiability gaps. This lifts multi-view identifiability algebras and sparse-intervention code design from objects to articulated structures, improving recovery under self-occlusion and reducing required episodes.

result.text: Epistemic OT-gated specialist curriculum for RL: couple uncertainty-aware MoE routing with an optimal-transport curriculum that progressively moves the training context distribution along Wasserstein geodesics toward high-disagreement regime centers discovered by an ensemble (epistemic POMDP). Train a soft MoE policy/value whose router temperature is modulated by predictive disagreement and whose experts are diversity-regularized via orthogonalization; when persistent regime clusters appear, spawn specialists initialized from the MoE subspace, train them on the corresponding curriculum stages, and distill their behavior back into the MoE to prevent the generalist plateau. The curriculum is recomputed online as beliefs shift, and in nonstationary streams a GP-style mixture dynamics model triggers change-point updates and specialist reactivation. This unifies curriculum shaping, uncertainty-conditioned routing, and generalist–specialist transfer to improve zero-shot generalization and sample efficiency on procedurally diverse and drifting benchmarks.

args.text: We propose Structured Scene-Graph Energy Decoding (SSED), a training-free controller that steers LVLM generation with a global scene-level objective. At each step, SSED builds a provisional text scene graph from the partial output and scores it against a visual graph composed from open-vocabulary detectors and HOI predictors using an energy that (i) penalizes unsupported nodes/relations, (ii) rewards coverage of high-confidence objects with a budgeted, non-duplicative set term, and (iii) enforces mutual consistency among triplets. This energy augments HALC-style local grounding with global beam re-ranking, suppressing spurious objects and predicates while preserving fluency; we expect measurable gains on multi-object benchmarks like ROPE and relation-focused suites. SSED unifies ideas from detector-guided grounding and post-hoc rescoring into a single decoding-time structure, requiring no retraining.

We propose spatio-temporal identifiability for object-centric multi-view videos under occlusion without labeled interventions: temporal sparsity of changes acts as implicit, slot-targeted perturbations. Under compositional-and-irreducible object generative processes and instance-dependent partial observability, if the time-augmented co-visibility graph is pairwise-connected across short windows and at most s slots change per step, object latents are identifiable up to slot permutation via contrastive multi-view encoding with a per-slot sparse temporal-difference prior. We instantiate a slot-contrastive encoder with cycle-consistency across time–view edges and a SlowVAE-like group-sparsity penalty on per-slot deltas to detect which slot changed, yielding identifiability guarantees and improved recovery in heavily occluded natural videos. This unifies multi-view shared-information algebra, object-centric identifiability, and temporal sparsity into a single framework.

result.text: Current query-aware KV paging reduces loads by scoring existing cache pages, but page boundaries are incidental to sequence order; as a result, attention mass is fragmented across many pages. We propose AttnPack, a learned KV cache layout that repacks keys/values into pagelets so that tokens frequently co-attended for real queries are co-located, using normalized-attention statistics and retrieval-time co-access to build a co-attention graph and solve a size-constrained partitioning. Plugged under Quest-style selectors and Sparse RAG’s per-document gating, AttnPack cuts page fan-out so top-K pages cover most saliency, while a tiny recurrent summary (LESS-style) shadows evicted clusters to preserve recoverability. This co-design of paging and layout targets large IO and latency reductions without retraining, and can be maintained incrementally for streaming inputs.

result.text: We propose hierarchical object–part causal representation learning under multi-view partial observability and occlusion, where each object is modeled as a tree-structured assembly of parts connected by kinematic constraints. We show that identifiability of part-wise causal latents and cross-view correspondences holds (up to per-part reparameterizations and tree automorphisms) if the part-level co-visibility hypergraph is pairwise-connected across episodes and either instance-dependent sparsity of part visibility provides sufficient support variation or occasional sparse, unlabeled joint-targeted perturbations occur. Algorithmically, we instantiate a multi-view slot-to-part encoder that enforces cycle-consistent matching on the part co-visibility graph and kinematic-cycle consistency on the tree, with a change-anchoring causal loss at the part level; an active designer selects next views and joint perturbations to close algebra-predicted identifiability gaps. This lifts multi-view identifiability algebras and sparse-intervention code design from objects to articulated structures, improving recovery under self-occlusion and reducing required episodes.

result.text: We propose Structured Scene-Graph Energy Decoding (SSED), a training-free controller that steers LVLM generation with a global scene-level objective. At each step, SSED builds a provisional text scene graph from the partial output and scores it against a visual graph composed from open-vocabulary detectors and HOI predictors using an energy that (i) penalizes unsupported nodes/relations, (ii) rewards coverage of high-confidence objects with a budgeted, non-duplicative set term, and (iii) enforces mutual consistency among triplets. This energy augments HALC-style local grounding with global beam re-ranking, suppressing spurious objects and predicates while preserving fluency; we expect measurable gains on multi-object benchmarks like ROPE and relation-focused suites. SSED unifies ideas from detector-guided grounding and post-hoc rescoring into a single decoding-time structure, requiring no retraining.

result.text: The paper studies CountSketch’s vulnerability when inputs are chosen adaptively—i.e., later vectors can depend on earlier sketch outputs—which models feedback loops and adversarial queries, and shows the standard estimator can be broken with about as many queries as the sketch dimension. result.text: We propose MoSA: Mixture-of-Shift Adaptation for unlabeled test-time streams that explicitly disentangles and schedules two update paths—label-prior reweighting and covariate adaptation—based on online evidence of the dominant shift. MoSA maintains streaming estimates of class priors via no-label label-shift learners while feeding a safe, small-step entropy–sharpness covariate update stabilized by per-layer BN interpolation and gated by OOD/gradient filters; a prediction-balanced reservoir breaks temporal correlations to make both estimators reliable. At each step, a tiny convex selector chooses mixture weights between prior reweighting and feature updates to minimize a proxy risk subject to stability constraints, preventing forgetting and collapse under small, non-i.i.d. batches. This unified controller should reduce regret versus single-mechanism TTA under mixed shifts and yields practical robustness across batch sizes and streaming conditions.

result.text: The paper addresses the tension in conformal prediction between achieving conditional validity (accurate coverage for subpopulations or under covariate shift) and producing prediction sets that are as short/informative as possible. The key insight is that one can pose prediction-set construction as a length-optimization problem subject to conditional-coverage constraints and that, under broad covariate-shift classes (including marginal and group-conditional settings), this constrained optimization admits strong duality in the infinite-sample limit so that (near-)optimal-length sets that satisfy conditional validity can be realized. The authors propose the CPL (Conformal Prediction with Length-Optimization) framework which operationalizes this idea by solving the dual-informed optimization in practice, proving finite-sample conditional validity guarantees, and demonstrating empirically across classification, regression, and LLM-based multiple-choice tasks that CPL yields substantially smaller prediction sets than prior methods while maintaining the desired coverage properties.

result.text: The paper addresses hallucinations in large vision-language models (LVLMs), where generated text can diverge from image content, noting that existing visual contrastive decoding methods fail to reliably suppress hallucinatory tokens due to uncontrolled global visual uncertainty. The key insight is that contrastive decoding’s effectiveness depends on precisely amplifying the preference gap between hallucinated and target tokens, which can be achieved by replacing noisy global uncertainty signals with a learned, theoretically grounded preference model to more accurately identify and penalize hallucinatory outputs. The authors propose Hallucination-Induced Optimization (HIO), which fine-tunes a Contrary Bradley-Terry preference model to amplify contrasts between hallucinatory and correct tokens and then uses this model to guide contrastive decoding, thereby more effectively discouraging hallucinations. Experiments across multiple benchmarks show HIO reduces hallucinations and outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of optimizing reinforcement learning policies to maximally satisfy Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) specifications, where standard RL’s myopic reward-based learning struggles to find policies with highest long-run satisfaction probability. The key insight is that by introducing an “eventual discounting” value-function proxy one can align value-based optimization with maximizing the probability of satisfying LTL formulas, and that additional learning signal can be obtained by imagining alternate futures in which different satisfaction paths occurred. result.text: The paper addresses why reinforcement learning agents often fail to generalize from limited training environments to unseen test conditions, arguing that the sequential decision-making setting creates a distinct challenge not captured by supervised-learning generalization analysis. The key insight is that uncertainty about which training conditions will occur at test time induces implicit partial observability—turning nominally fully observed MDPs into “epistemic POMDPs” whose hidden state encodes epistemic uncertainty about environment parameters. The authors formalize this epistemic POMDP and show that methods ignoring the induced partial observability fail, then propose a simple ensemble-based approach that approximates inference over the hidden epistemic state and thereby better conditions policies on uncertainty. Empirically, their ensemble-derived method significantly improves generalization on Procgen compared to baselines, supporting the view that RL generalization requires explicitly addressing epistemic partial observability.

result.text: We propose CoTTA-C: a conformal-triggered, safe test-time adaptation wrapper that maintains online prediction-set coverage certificates and triggers updates only when coverage or a martingale-detected shift in entropy-based nonconformity departs from the source regime. Upon trigger, CoTTA-C routes adaptation along one of two paths: label-prior recalibration using no-label online label-shift estimators, or covariate adaptation using high-confidence, class-uniform filtering with sharpness-aware entropy minimization under a Fisher trust region. Each micro-update is validated on a small reservoir by checking recovery of target coverage and the nonconformity distribution; failing updates are rolled back to prevent collapse. This yields robust, calibrated TTA that adapts only when necessary and disentangles label vs. covariate shift while remaining efficient.

result.text: The paper tackles the persistent failure of monocular multi-object trackers to bridge long occlusions (over ~3s), noting that current appearance-driven methods recover less than 10% of such gaps; the key insight is that predicting likely future trajectories for moving agents dramatically constrains the association search space during long-term occlusions. The authors therefore integrate bird’s-eye-view trajectory forecasting that produces a small, diverse set of plausible future paths with associated localization uncertainty, and use these forecasts to guide data association across extended occlusion intervals. Implemented on top of existing trackers and evaluated on MOTChallenge, this method substantially improves long-term tracking robustness by reducing false re-associations and recovering many more long-gap identities, demonstrating that trajectory reasoning is a crucial component for long-term multi-object tracking.

result.text: The paper tackles task-agnostic continual online reinforcement learning where an agent must continually solve unseen, nonstationary tasks from streaming data without access to task labels, pretraining on a known task distribution, or clear task boundaries. Its key insight is to model changing dynamics as an infinite mixture of Gaussian Process experts, so the system can both flexibly create new dynamics models when novel regimes appear and efficiently reuse existing ones while quantifying uncertainty for model-based planning. Methodologically, the authors maintain a mixture-of-experts dynamics model with each expert implemented as a Gaussian Process, introduce a temporal transition prior to capture dependencies in the data stream, and update the mixture online via sequential variational inference so new components can be spawned or old ones reactivated; this model-based RL pipeline is then used for planning and demonstrated to outperform baselines on nonstationary control and driving tasks.

args.text: We propose Bandit-TTA: a nonstationary contextual-bandit controller that adaptively schedules among a small toolkit of adaptation primitives—no-update, label-prior reweighting, sharpness-aware entropy minimization, and forward-only prompt/activation shifts—based on online signals from the test stream. A prediction-balanced reservoir and a betting-martingale shift detector govern when to explore vs. exploit; the chosen arm must improve a proxy reward (validated entropy/calibration on the reservoir) while respecting switching-cost regularization and maintaining online conformal coverage constraints, with rollback on detected harm. This framing yields dynamic-regret-style guarantees under bounded drift and naturally favors FOA when backprop is infeasible and label-shift reweighting when priors drift, reducing collapse and forgetting under mixed, non-i.i.d. conditions. By casting TTA as bandit scheduling over diverse mechanisms with safety guards, Bandit-TTA unifies robust adaptation and principled triggering while remaining resource-aware.

result.text: The paper studies the “modality gap,” a geometric phenomenon where different data modalities (e.g., images and text) occupy distinct, arm’s-length regions in the shared embedding space of multi-modal contrastive models like CLIP, which can hinder downstream performance and fairness. The key insight is that this gap arises from two interacting causes: (1) standard neural network initialization biases each encoder’s outputs into a narrow cone so that different encoders start separated, and (2) contrastive optimization—particularly the temperature hyperparameter—preserves or enforces a nonzero separation between modalities during training. To analyze and mitigate this, the authors combine empirical measurement and theoretical analysis of initialization-induced concentration with controlled contrastive training experiments that vary temperature and alignment forces, showing that adjusting the modality gap can substantially affect zero-shot classification accuracy and fairness outcomes.

args.text: We propose self-calibrating object-centric multi-view causal representation learning under occlusion, where camera extrinsics are unknown and may drift across episodes. We show that slots and poses are identifiable up to a joint similarity transform when the time-augmented co-visibility hypergraph provides sufficient cycle coverage to synchronize views, and sparse unlabeled interventions or temporal sparsity supply per-slot change anchors—extending the multi-view identifiability algebra to jointly recover geometry and causal latents. Algorithmically, we couple a contrastive multi-view slot encoder with epipolar and cycle-consistency constraints and a bundle-adjustment-like pose head, while an active planner selects camera motions and perturbations that close algebra-predicted gaps in pose observability and slot RIP. This lifts object-centric identifiability to the calibration-free setting, reducing reliance on pre-calibration and improving robustness under heavy occlusion and camera drift.

result.text: The paper addresses the underutilization of unchosen experts in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, noting that simply activating more experts can degrade output and that different routing strategies produce substantially different, non-synergistic outputs. The key insight is that unchosen experts still contain useful signals and that contrasting outputs from different activation strengths can surface better next-token probabilities without changing model weights. The authors propose Self-Contrast Mixture-of-Experts (SCMoE), a training-free, inference-time method that computes next-token probabilities by contrasting outputs produced under strong versus weak expert activation of the same MoE model, incurring minimal extra latency. Experiments on multiple benchmarks (GSM8K, StrategyQA, MBPP, HumanEval) show consistent reasoning improvements for Mixtral 8x7B—e.g., GSM8K accuracy rising from 61.79 to 66.94—and further gains when combined with self-consistency.

result.text: We propose self-calibrating object-centric multi-view causal representation learning under occlusion, where camera extrinsics are unknown and may drift across episodes. We show that slots and poses are identifiable up to a joint similarity transform when the time-augmented co-visibility hypergraph provides sufficient cycle coverage to synchronize views, and sparse unlabeled interventions or temporal sparsity supply per-slot change anchors—extending the multi-view identifiability algebra to jointly recover geometry and causal latents. Algorithmically, we couple a contrastive multi-view slot encoder with epipolar and cycle-consistency constraints and a bundle-adjustment-like pose head, while an active planner selects camera motions and perturbations that close algebra-predicted gaps in pose observability and slot RIP. This lifts object-centric identifiability to the calibration-free setting, reducing reliance on pre-calibration and improving robustness under heavy occlusion and camera drift.

result.text: We propose CoTTA-C: a conformal-triggered, safe test-time adaptation wrapper that maintains online prediction-set coverage certificates and triggers updates only when coverage or a martingale-detected shift in entropy-based nonconformity departs from the source regime. Upon trigger, CoTTA-C routes adaptation along one of two paths: label-prior recalibration using no-label online label-shift estimators, or covariate adaptation using high-confidence, class-uniform filtering with sharpness-aware entropy minimization under a Fisher trust region. Each micro-update is validated on a small reservoir by checking recovery of target coverage and the nonconformity distribution; failing updates are rolled back to prevent collapse. This yields robust, calibrated TTA that adapts only when necessary and disentangles label vs. covariate shift while remaining efficient.

result.text: We propose Counterfactual-Grounded Contrastive Decoding (CGCD) for LVLMs, which unifies token-level causal visual grounding with internal-activation trust signals to suppress object hallucinations at test time. At each decoding step, CGCD estimates a causal grounding score for candidate object/attribute tokens by grouping visual tokens into regions and measuring logit deltas under region-masking counterfactuals, then fuses this with sharpness/consistency statistics from hidden states to quantify hallucination risk. The risk adaptively subtracts penalties from candidate logits and guides a global beam re-ranking pass, while a lightweight co-occurrence prior only penalizes late, low-grounding mentions to avoid hurting fluency. This plug-and-play procedure amortizes cost via grouped perturbations and early token pruning, and is expected to outperform SID/HALC/LURE by only suppressing prior-driven tokens when internal evidence indicates ungroundedness.
